scenario: You are leading a cross-functional initiative, but a peer manager in another department is consistently deprioritizing their team's deliverables for your project, citing competing internal goals.

options.text: Schedule a 1-on-1 with the peer manager to understand their competing goals, find areas of mutual benefit, and negotiate a revised, realistic timeline for their deliverables.
Escalate the issue to the executive sponsor of the initiative, asking them to force the peer manager to comply.
Reassign the peer manager's deliverables to your own team to ensure the project stays on track, even if it causes your team to overwork.
Bring up the delays in the next cross-functional status meeting to publicly pressure the peer manager into delivering.

scenario: A frontline manager who reports to you is struggling to transition from an individual contributor mindset, often micromanaging their team and creating bottlenecks.

options.text: Tell them to step back and stop micromanaging, warning them that their team's morale is at risk.
Take over some of the frontline manager's approval duties to alleviate the bottleneck and keep the team moving.
Provide targeted coaching on delegation, help them identify tasks they can hand off immediately, and set clear expectations for their role as a leader.
Enroll them in a generalized leadership training program and hope it resolves the issue.

scenario: A VP has proposed a new 'pet project' for your department. Based on your analysis, it is resource-heavy, lacks strategic alignment, and will derail your current KPIs.

options.text: Accept the project without pushback since it comes from a VP, and instruct your team to do their best.
Present the VP with a data-driven impact analysis showing the risks to current KPIs, and propose an alternative, scaled-down pilot that aligns better with current capacity.
Politely decline the project via email, stating that your department is currently at capacity.
Agree to the project but intentionally under-resource it, focusing on your main KPIs instead.

scenario: Your company announces a major restructuring. Your department's scope is expanding significantly, but you have been told there will be no additional headcount for the next two quarters.

options.text: Gather your management team to audit current projects, ruthlessly deprioritize low-impact work, and redesign workflows to absorb the new scope sustainably.
Complain to leadership that the mandate is impossible, hoping they will reconsider the headcount freeze.
Tell your team they will just have to work longer hours for the next six months to get through the transition.
Accept the new scope but quietly let deadlines slip on the new responsibilities to prove you need more people.

scenario: An employee two levels down from you (reporting to one of your managers) comes directly to you with a complaint about their manager's leadership style.

options.text: Listen to their concerns to make them feel heard, but instruct them to resolve it directly with their manager without getting involved.
Immediately confront your direct report (their manager) with the employee's complaints and demand an explanation.
Listen actively, ask probing questions to separate facts from feelings, and then coach the employee on how to have a constructive feedback conversation with their manager.
Offer to mediate a sit-down meeting between the employee and their manager right away.

scenario: You need to secure buy-in from several department heads to adopt a new, standardized software platform, but many are resistant because they prefer their current bespoke tools.

options.text: Mandate the change, citing executive authority, and give them a strict 30-day deadline to transition.
Identify a department head who is moderately receptive, partner with them to run a successful pilot, and use those results to influence the remaining holdouts.
Host a large presentation highlighting all the features of the new software and ask for a vote.
Meet with them individually to argue why their current tools are inferior and inefficient.

scenario: Two of your most senior team leads are constantly arguing over resource allocation and territorial boundaries, creating a toxic environment for the broader team.

options.text: Bring them into a joint meeting, establish clear boundaries yourself, and mandate that they collaborate strictly within those parameters.
Facilitate a mediation session where they must align on shared department goals, identify the root cause of the friction, and co-create an SLA for resource sharing.
Let them sort it out themselves, as senior leaders should be able to resolve their own conflicts.
Threaten to reduce both of their budgets if they cannot learn to play nice.

scenario: You are presenting the results of a high-profile initiative to the executive board. The initiative failed to meet its primary ROI targets due to unforeseen market shifts.

options.text: Gloss over the missed targets and focus entirely on the secondary metrics that were successful.
Own the results transparently, present a clear post-mortem analysis of the market shifts, and outline a pivot strategy to recapture value.
Blame the failure on the sales and marketing teams for not adapting to the market shifts quickly enough.
Apologize profusely for the failure and ask the board what they would like you to do next.

scenario: A highly talented but abrasive senior engineer on your team is alienating junior staff and causing high turnover in their immediate pod.

options.text: Isolate the senior engineer so they only work on solo projects, minimizing their interaction with junior staff.
Have a direct conversation explicitly tying their behavioral issues to their performance review, setting clear expectations for professional conduct and offering coaching.
Ignore the behavior because their technical output is too valuable to the company to risk upsetting them.
Fire the senior engineer immediately to send a message about company culture.

scenario: You notice that your department's diversity metrics have stagnated, and underrepresented groups are not advancing to leadership roles at the same rate as their peers.

options.text: Launch a targeted mentorship and sponsorship program pairing high-potential underrepresented employees with senior leaders, while auditing your promotion criteria for bias.
Mandate that the next three leadership hires must come from underrepresented backgrounds, regardless of the applicant pool.
Send an email to the department emphasizing the importance of diversity and inclusion.
Ask HR to investigate the issue and wait for their recommendations before taking any action.

scenario: A peer manager in a critical support function is hoarding information, refusing to share data that your team needs to optimize its operations.

options.text: Go to their boss and explain that this manager is being uncooperative and hurting the business.
Have a candid conversation with the peer to understand their hesitation (e.g., data privacy, fear of misuse), and establish a secure, mutually beneficial data-sharing agreement.
Retaliate by withholding your team's support from their future initiatives until they share the data.
Try to bypass the manager by asking their direct reports for the data informally.

scenario: Your organization is shifting from a fully remote model to a hybrid model (3 days in-office). Many of your team members are highly resistant and threatening to quit.

options.text: Tell them it's a corporate mandate and out of your hands, and they must comply or leave.
Hold a town hall to acknowledge their frustrations, explain the business rationale transparently, and empower team leads to determine the most flexible, effective schedule within the mandate.
Secretly tell your top performers they can continue working fully remotely to prevent them from quitting.
Advocate aggressively to executive leadership to reverse the policy for your specific department.

scenario: You have identified a significant inefficiency in a legacy process that spans three different departments. Changing it requires upfront work from everyone, but only benefits your department directly.

options.text: Demand the change be made because it makes the company as a whole more efficient.
Map out the new process and present it to the other department heads, focusing on how you can offset their upfront effort or find secondary benefits for their teams.
Implement a workaround strictly within your own department, leaving the legacy process intact for the others.
Complain to upper management about the legacy process and ask them to mandate the change.

scenario: One of your newly promoted team leads is struggling with imposter syndrome and avoiding making difficult decisions, deferring everything back to you.

options.text: Continue making the decisions for them to ensure the business doesn't suffer while they adjust to the role.
Demote them back to their previous role, explaining they aren't quite ready for leadership.
Implement a 'bring me solutions, not just problems' rule, asking them to propose a decision and their rationale before you weigh in, gradually rebuilding their confidence.
Tell them to trust their gut and refuse to answer their questions so they are forced to decide.

scenario: A key stakeholder is notorious for moving the goalposts late in a project, causing budget overruns and team burnout. A new project with them is just starting.

options.text: Refuse to take on the project unless the stakeholder is replaced.
Establish a rigid change-control process upfront, requiring the stakeholder's signature and a budget/timeline impact review for any scope changes past the initial kickoff.
Buffer all your estimates by 50% without telling them, anticipating the inevitable scope creep.
Warn the stakeholder verbally that you will not accept any late changes this time.

scenario: Your department just went through a round of layoffs. The remaining team members are anxious, demoralized, and worried about their own job security.

options.text: Hold an open forum to address their fears honestly, clarify the company's financial standing and strategic path forward, and collaboratively reset priorities given the reduced headcount.
Act relentlessly positive and tell them they are lucky to still have jobs, urging them to focus on the future.
Avoid discussing the layoffs entirely and immediately dive into the next quarter's OKRs.
Promise them categorically that there will be no more layoffs, even if you cannot guarantee it.

scenario: You are leading a team meeting and a junior employee proposes an idea that completely contradicts the strategy you just laid out.

options.text: Shut the idea down immediately to maintain authority and keep the meeting on track.
Thank them for their input, ask them to expand on their reasoning to foster psychological safety, and respectfully discuss the trade-offs relative to the current strategy.
Tell them you will take it offline and then never follow up.
Change the strategy on the spot to show you are an open-minded and flexible leader.

scenario: A highly visible project managed by your department is failing. Executive leadership demands an explanation and an immediate fix.

options.text: Throw the project manager under the bus, assuring leadership you will closely manage them from now on.
Take ultimate responsibility, present a root-cause analysis without blaming individuals, and outline a specific, 30-day turnaround plan with new milestone checks.
Downplay the severity of the failure and ask for more time and money to fix it.
Defend the project, arguing that the executives' expectations were unrealistic to begin with.

scenario: You oversee two managers whose teams have highly interdependent workflows. Recently, miscommunications between the teams have led to missed deliverables.

options.text: Bring both managers together to map the joint workflow, identify the communication breakdowns, and establish a shared dashboard or daily sync to ensure alignment.
Take over the coordination between the two teams yourself to ensure no more deliverables are missed.
Merge the two teams into one under a single manager to eliminate the boundary altogether.
Send a formal warning to both managers that further missed deliverables will impact their bonuses.

scenario: You are advocating for a new strategic initiative, but the CFO is skeptical of the ROI and blocking the funding.

options.text: Give up on the initiative and tell your team that Finance killed the project.
Partner with a finance analyst to build a more robust, conservative financial model, addressing the CFO's specific risk concerns, and re-pitch the initiative as a phased pilot.
Try to fund the initiative by secretly siphoning budget from other approved projects.
Go to the CEO directly and complain that the CFO is blocking innovation.

scenario: Your organization is pushing a new set of corporate values, but your team feels they are disconnected from the day-to-day reality of the work.

options.text: Agree with your team that the values are just 'corporate fluff' and ignore them.
Facilitate a workshop with your team to translate the high-level corporate values into tangible, actionable behaviors and norms specific to your department's daily work.
Print posters of the values and hang them in the office, hoping they passively absorb them.
Incorporate the corporate values strictly into the next performance review cycle without prior discussion.

scenario: A talented manager on your team has high turnover in their department. Exit interviews consistently cite a lack of career growth and mentorship.

options.text: Fire the manager, as high turnover is an unacceptable metric.
Review the exit interview data with the manager, co-create a development plan focused on their coaching skills, and mandate quarterly career conversations with all their direct reports.
Take over the career development conversations for their team members yourself.
Advise the manager to hire less ambitious people who won't care as much about career growth.

scenario: You need to select a vendor for a major software upgrade. Your team strongly prefers Vendor A, but executive leadership has a pre-existing relationship with Vendor B and is nudging you in that direction.

options.text: Choose Vendor B immediately to please executive leadership, ignoring your team's preference.
Conduct a rigorous, objective evaluation of both vendors against a pre-defined scorecard, and present the data-driven recommendation to leadership, highlighting risks and benefits.
Choose Vendor A without consulting leadership, asserting your authority as the decision-maker.
Ask leadership to make the final decision themselves so you cannot be blamed if it fails.

scenario: A critical, urgent project drops into your lap on a Friday afternoon, requiring weekend work from your already exhausted team.

options.text: Send a mass email demanding everyone work the weekend, offering no explanation or compensation.
Push back on the urgency entirely and refuse to do the work until Monday morning.
Determine exactly what absolute minimum viable product is needed by Monday, jump in to help execute it yourself, and arrange comp time or bonuses for those who assist.
Ask for volunteers and do the rest of the work entirely by yourself to protect your team.

scenario: You suspect a manager reporting to you is showing favoritism toward a specific employee, giving them the best assignments and highest bonuses despite average performance.

options.text: Confront the manager with your observations, review the objective performance data and assignment logs together, and coach them on equitable management practices.
Publicly call out the favoritism in the next leadership team meeting.
Reassign the favored employee to a different manager to eliminate the problem.
Overrule the manager's bonus recommendations and normalize the ratings without discussing it with them.

scenario: Your organization is launching a sweeping AI transformation. Most of your team is excited, but a few veteran employees are deeply cynical and vocally resisting the change.

options.text: Tell the cynics they need to get on board or look for a new job.
Engage the cynics privately to understand their underlying concerns (e.g., job security, learning curve), validate their experience, and involve them in testing the new AI tools.
Ignore the cynics and focus all your energy on the early adopters.
Slow down the entire transformation process until the cynics feel comfortable.

scenario: During a performance calibration meeting with your peers, another mid-level manager unfairly criticizes one of your top performers based on a single isolated incident.

options.text: Retaliate by aggressively criticizing one of their top performers.
Remain calm, acknowledge the incident they mentioned, but provide a comprehensive set of data and 360-feedback that proves a sustained pattern of high performance.
Yield to the peer's criticism to avoid conflict and lower your employee's rating.
Interrupt the peer and accuse them of being biased and unprofessional.

scenario: You are stepping into a new role managing a team that was deeply loyal to their previous manager, who was recently fired for poor performance.

options.text: Badmouth the previous manager to justify their firing and establish your superiority.
Acknowledge the transition is difficult, set clear expectations going forward, and focus on building trust through consistent support and quick, visible wins for the team.
Change all of the previous manager's processes immediately to wipe the slate clean.
Try to act exactly like the previous manager so the team feels comfortable.

scenario: Your department is chronically understaffed, and HR is taking months to fill open requisitions, causing significant strain on your team.

options.text: Yell at the HR recruiting team for being incompetent.
Partner with HR to understand their bottlenecks, offer your team's subject matter experts to help source or screen candidates, and build a collaborative hiring pipeline.
Stop taking on new work entirely until the roles are filled.
Bypass HR entirely and hire contractors using a corporate credit card.

scenario: A highly innovative project proposed by your team requires breaking several rigid, outdated internal IT security policies.

options.text: Proceed with the project in secret, bypassing IT security protocols (Shadow IT).
Collaborate with the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) to demonstrate the business value of the project and co-design a secure, compliant workaround or exception.
Scrap the project entirely since it violates current policy.
Escalate the issue to the CEO to force IT to change their policies.

scenario: You overhear a manager reporting to you making an insensitive remark that borders on discrimination during a team lunch.

options.text: Ignore it since it happened in a casual setting outside the office.
Pull them aside immediately after lunch, clearly state that the comment was inappropriate and violates company values, and involve HR for formal documentation and training.
Publicly berate them in front of the team to show you are an ally.
Wait until their annual performance review to mention that their communication style needs work.

scenario: Your team's morale has taken a hit because senior leadership frequently cancels your department's town halls and seems inaccessible.

options.text: Tell your team that senior leadership doesn't care about them.
Step into the communication void by hosting your own regular 'Ask Me Anything' sessions, proactively sourcing updates from leadership to cascade down to your team.
Send an angry email to the CEO demanding they show up to the next town hall.
Cancel your own team meetings as well, since communication doesn't seem to be a priority.

scenario: You have been asked to lead a tiger team to fix a critical operational failure, but the team comprises senior experts who are skeptical of your technical knowledge.

options.text: Try to fake technical expertise and aggressively debate them to prove you belong in charge.

Acknowledge their superior technical expertise, clearly define your role as the facilitator and unblocker, and empower them to drive the technical solutions while you manage stakeholder communication.
Delegate the entire project to the most vocal expert and take a backseat.
Micromanage their schedule and tasks to exert authority over the process.

scenario: You have recently been promoted to a mid-level management role, but you are still holding onto the day-to-day tactical tasks you excelled at as a frontline manager, causing you to work long hours.

options.text: Identify which of your old tasks align with the development goals of your new direct reports, provide them with the necessary context, and formally transition the ownership to them.
Continue doing the tactical tasks yourself, as training someone else will take more time than you currently have to spare.
Slowly hand off the tasks one by one over the next year to ensure the quality doesn't drop during the transition.
Distribute all your old tasks evenly across your team immediately without checking their current capacity, telling them it is part of their new scope.

scenario: A frontline manager who reports to you is becoming a bottleneck. They insist on reviewing every piece of work their team produces before it goes out, leading to missed deadlines.

options.text: Tell them to stop reviewing the work immediately and just trust their team, regardless of the quality implications.
Take over the review process yourself so the frontline manager has more time to focus on strategy.
Coach the manager on implementing a tiered review system, where they only review high-risk deliverables while empowering their team to self-approve routine work.
Suggest they hire an additional team member to help handle the massive volume of reviews.

scenario: You have been asked to present a highly visible quarterly update to the executive board. One of your top-performing team leads is ready for a stretch assignment and wants more executive exposure.

options.text: Delegate the creation and delivery of the presentation to the team lead, offering to review their drafts and hold a practice session to ensure they are set up for success.
Create the presentation yourself, but allow the team lead to sit in the back of the room during the executive meeting to watch you deliver it.
Decline to involve them, as executive presentations are strictly the responsibility of mid-level managers and above.
Have the team lead build all the slides, but deliver the presentation yourself so the executives hear it from you.

scenario: A critical project managed by one of your newly empowered teams is slightly behind schedule. The team is aware and working on a recovery plan, but you are feeling anxious about the delay.

options.text: Step in immediately, take over the project management, and start assigning daily tasks to get it back on track.
Request a status meeting to review their recovery plan, ask probing questions to ensure it is robust, and offer your support in clearing any higher-level roadblocks.
Send a strong email reminding them of the deadline and warning them of the consequences if they fail.
Leave them completely alone and do not ask for updates, trusting that they will figure it out eventually.

scenario: You inherit a team that is used to a highly directive, micromanaging boss. They currently wait for explicit instructions before starting any task and refuse to make independent decisions.

options.text: Continue operating with strict directives so the team feels comfortable, as changing their culture will cause too much disruption.
Gradually introduce autonomy by assigning small, low-risk decisions to the team, openly celebrating their successes and framing mistakes as learning opportunities.
Announce that they are fully autonomous now and refuse to answer their questions to force them to be independent.
Assign them a massive, high-stakes project immediately to test their ability to step up.

scenario: A manager on your team makes an autonomous decision regarding a vendor contract that results in a minor financial loss, though it was a well-intentioned, calculated risk.

options.text: Revoke their decision-making authority for future contracts to prevent any further financial losses.
Discuss the outcome privately to analyze what went wrong, reinforce your support for their initiative, and extract lessons learned for future decisions.
Ignore the financial loss entirely so they don't feel bad about making the mistake.
Require them to get your written approval for all vendor contracts moving forward.

scenario: A senior stakeholder frequently bypasses your empowered team lead and comes directly to you with project requests and questions.

options.text: Answer the stakeholder's questions yourself to provide good customer service, but cc the team lead on your responses.
Tell the stakeholder to stop bothering you and talk to the team lead.
Politely redirect the stakeholder to the team lead, reinforcing the lead's authority, and privately ensure the lead is equipped to handle the stakeholder's requests.
Take over the project entirely since the stakeholder clearly prefers working with you.

scenario: You need to delegate the annual budgeting process for your department. You have a capable subordinate, but they have never managed a budget of this scale before.

options.text: Delegate the task but schedule weekly milestone check-ins, provide the previous year's templates, and clearly define the strategic priorities they should align the budget to.
Do the budget yourself this year and promise to teach them how to do it next year.
Give them the task and tell them the final draft is due in a month, offering no further guidance.
Have them do the easiest parts of the budget (like software renewals) while you handle the complex forecasting.

scenario: You delegated a project to a highly competent direct report. When reviewing their final deliverable, you notice they took a completely different approach than you would have, though the outcome meets all requirements.

options.text: Praise them for meeting the objective, ask them to walk you through their approach to learn from their perspective, and accept the deliverable as is.
Make them redo the project using your preferred approach so it aligns with your specific standards.
Accept the deliverable but rewrite parts of it yourself so it looks more like your own work.
Tell them their approach was wrong but you will accept it this one time to save the schedule.

scenario: You oversee a remote, distributed team across multiple time zones. They are currently struggling to make progress because they are waiting for you to log online and approve their daily tasks.

options.text: Establish clear boundaries of authority, transition from task-based management to outcome-based management, and empower them to proceed with work within agreed-upon parameters without your daily sign-off.
Change your personal working hours to span across all their time zones so you can approve things faster.
Appoint a single 'deputy' in a central time zone who must approve all work when you are offline.
Tell them to just find busywork to do while they wait for your approvals.

scenario: You want to delegate a complex stretch assignment to an employee who is fully capable, but they express deep fear of failing and ruining their reputation.

options.text: Acknowledge their hesitation, frame the assignment as a collaborative growth opportunity, set up a 'safety net' of regular check-ins, and explicitly state that you share accountability for the outcome.
Tell them they lack confidence and give the assignment to someone else who is more ambitious.
Force them to take the assignment, telling them it's mandatory for their job security.
Break the assignment down into smaller, less intimidating pieces, though this means they miss out on the full leadership experience.

scenario: Your department must complete a tedious, manual administrative audit that provides no strategic value or skill development. You need to assign it to your team.

options.text: Pretend the task is a highly prestigious leadership opportunity to trick a junior employee into volunteering for it.

Acknowledge the tedious nature of the task transparently, distribute the workload evenly across the entire team (including yourself) to minimize the burden, and challenge the team to find a way to automate it for next time.
Dump the entire task on your newest hire, as it is a rite of passage.
Ask for a single volunteer and promise them an extra day off if they do it all themselves.

scenario: You fully empowered a squad to define their own quarterly roadmap, but halfway through the quarter, you realize their goals have drifted significantly away from the company's core strategic OKRs.

options.text: Revoke their autonomy entirely and dictate their roadmap for the remainder of the year.
Hold a realignment session to review the company OKRs together, discuss where the gap occurred, and collaboratively pivot their current roadmap back toward strategic alignment.
Let them finish out the quarter on their current trajectory to preserve their sense of autonomy, even if the work doesn't align.
Micromanage their daily standups to slowly steer them back on track without explicitly telling them they drifted.

scenario: You notice that a manager reporting to you is 'dumping' tasks on their team—assigning work via brief emails with zero context, deadlines, or support—which is causing team frustration.

options.text: Ignore the issue as long as the work is eventually getting done by the team.
Coach the manager on the difference between abdication and delegation, providing them with a framework for setting context, defining success, and providing necessary resources.
Bypass the manager and provide the context to their team directly.
Reprimand the manager publicly during a team meeting to show the team you have their backs.

scenario: A critical system goes down. You are the subject matter expert, but you are currently double-booked with a high-priority executive offsite. You have a senior engineer capable of handling it.

options.text: Cancel your executive offsite and fix the system yourself, as it's too critical to trust to anyone else.
Delegate the crisis response fully to the senior engineer, provide them with the authority to pull in necessary resources, and ask them to text you hourly updates.
Tell the engineer to fix it, but insist they call you to approve every single technical command they run.
Let the system stay down until you are out of your offsite.

scenario: Your team constantly escalates minor budgetary decisions (e.g., $50 software licenses, $100 team lunches) to you for approval, clogging your inbox.

options.text: Complain to finance that they need to make the approval system easier for you to use.
Establish a clear policy that empowers team leads to pre-approve any expenditures under $500 that fit within their allocated budget, requiring your review only for exceptions.
Ban all minor expenditures so you don't have to deal with the approvals anymore.
Tell them to keep sending them, but just bulk-approve them without reading at the end of the week.

scenario: You are delegating the hiring process for an open role on a sub-team to the manager of that team. They are eager but have never made a final hiring decision.

options.text: Let them do the interviews, but tell them you will make the final decision on who gets the offer.
Equip them with interview rubrics and training, sit in on the interviews as an observer and advisor, but explicitly empower them to make the final hire.
Give them full control and do not participate at all, as that is true empowerment.
Take over the interviews because hiring is too risky to delegate to a novice manager.

scenario: You are preparing for a one-month sabbatical. You need to ensure your department runs smoothly in your absence without things falling apart or grinding to a halt.

options.text: Tell your team to pause all major initiatives and just maintain the status quo until you return.
Designate an acting leader, explicitly define their decision-making authority boundaries, brief stakeholders on the transition, and communicate escalation paths clearly to the team.
Tell everyone they are equally in charge and should manage by committee while you are gone.
Check your email for one hour a day during the sabbatical just to make sure nothing is on fire.

scenario: You want to empower your leadership team to develop the department's strategy for the next year, moving away from a top-down mandate approach.

options.text: Write the strategy yourself and then present it to them, asking for minor edits so they feel included.
Provide the overarching company goals and budget constraints, then facilitate a workshop where the leadership team brainstorms, debates, and finalizes the department's strategic initiatives.
Give them a blank whiteboard and tell them to figure out the strategy with zero input or constraints from you.
Assign each manager to write a separate strategy and then pick the one you like best.

scenario: An empowered project team is experiencing friction with a partner department over resource sharing. They ask you to intervene and resolve it for them.

options.text: Take over immediately and have a stern conversation with the partner department's director to fix the problem.
Tell the team they are empowered and must figure it out themselves without any of your help.
Coach the team on conflict resolution techniques, role-play the conversation with them, and empower them to negotiate a solution directly with the partner department.
Set up a meeting with the partner department and do most of the talking, but let your team sit in.

scenario: You notice a highly capable individual contributor is overwhelmed because various managers (including yourself) keep delegating high-priority tasks to them, recognizing their competence.

options.text: Tell them it is a compliment that everyone trusts them and encourage them to work harder.
Intervene to map their total capacity, help them ruthlessly prioritize, and route new requests through a central intake process to protect them from burnout.
Secretly tell them to ignore tasks from other managers and only focus on your delegated tasks.
Stop delegating to them entirely and give all your tasks to a less competent team member.

scenario: A project you completely delegated to a subordinate manager fails spectacularly, missing all deliverables and upsetting a major client.

options.text: Publicly blame the subordinate manager to the client, explaining that you delegated it to them and they failed.

Take full accountability for the failure as their leader, step in to manage the immediate client fallout, and conduct a private post-mortem with the manager to understand where the breakdown in oversight occurred.
Fire the manager immediately to show the client you are taking the failure seriously.
Fix the problem behind the scenes without telling the manager how severe the failure was.

scenario: You are leading a cross-functional squad. You notice the junior members are hesitant to speak up during brainstorming, always deferring to the senior architects.

options.text: Tell the senior architects to stop talking so the junior members can speak.
Implement structured brainstorming (like silent writing or round-robins) to equalize the floor, and explicitly assign junior members to lead specific research spikes to build their authority.
Accept that senior members should lead the ideation process naturally.
Talk to the junior members offline and relay their ideas for them in the meetings.

scenario: A direct report explicitly asks for more autonomy and less oversight, but they have missed two critical deadlines in the past month due to poor time management.

options.text: Give them the autonomy they are asking for, hoping the increased trust will motivate them to meet deadlines.
Have a transparent conversation explaining that autonomy is earned through reliability; set clear, near-term performance milestones they must hit to gradually earn that independence.
Deny the request bluntly and increase your micromanagement to ensure they never miss another deadline.
Give them autonomy on low-priority tasks only, but continue micromanaging their critical tasks without explaining why.

scenario: You need to delegate the onboarding and training of a critical new hire. You want the new hire to feel welcomed and get up to speed quickly.

options.text: Delegate the entire process to your most junior team member so they can practice leadership.
Do all the onboarding yourself because first impressions are too important to delegate.
Appoint a high-performing peer as their dedicated 'onboarding buddy', outline the key learning milestones, and schedule weekly check-ins with both of them to monitor progress.
Provide the new hire with a stack of documentation and empower them to self-onboard.

scenario: Your VP criticizes you for not knowing the exact technical details of a bug fix that your empowered engineering pod is currently resolving.

options.text: Apologize to the VP, dive deep into the code, and start attending every daily standup to ensure you know every detail moving forward.

Explain to the VP that you have delegated the tactical execution to a highly capable pod lead, outline the high-level mitigation strategy, and offer to bring the pod lead in for a technical deep-dive.
Tell the VP that as a mid-level manager, you shouldn't have to know technical details anymore.
Interrupt the pod lead's work to demand an exhaustive technical briefing so you can relay it to the VP.

scenario: Your empowered team is facing intense scope creep from a demanding internal client. They are struggling to say 'no' and are working late hours.

options.text: Tell the team they need to be tougher and figure out how to push back on their own.
Take over client communications entirely and tell the client that no further scope changes will be accepted.
Join their next client sync as a supportive sponsor, explicitly back the team's authority to enforce the project boundaries, and coach them offline on effective boundary-setting frameworks.
Advise the team to just accept the scope creep to keep the client happy.

scenario: You are delegating the negotiation of a software renewal contract to a manager on your team to build their vendor management skills.

options.text: Provide them with the target budget, non-negotiable legal terms, and your historical context, then empower them to run the negotiation up to the final signature.
Let them do the negotiation, but jump into the calls unannounced to correct them if they make a weak point.
Do the negotiation yourself because saving company money is more important than employee development.
Give them full authority with no guidance and tell them to get the best deal possible.

scenario: You notice that a manager reporting to you is taking all the public credit for a highly successful project that they completely delegated to their direct reports.

options.text: Praise the manager publicly, as successful delegation is a sign of good leadership and they are ultimately responsible.
Publicly correct the manager in a large meeting to ensure the individual contributors get the credit.
Coach the manager privately on the principle that true leaders shine the spotlight downward, and require them to highlight the specific ICs in the upcoming all-hands.
Email the individual contributors privately to thank them, but say nothing to the manager.

scenario: You want to foster a culture where your team feels empowered to take calculated risks and experiment, rather than always playing it safe.

options.text: Send an email telling everyone to 'fail fast' and start taking more risks.

Create a formal 'innovation sprint' where performance metrics are suspended, openly share your own past professional failures, and publicly reward the learning that comes from unsuccessful experiments.
Mandate that every team member must propose one radical idea per week or face a penalty.
Fund a small skunkworks project for your two top performers and leave the rest of the team as is.

scenario: Your portfolio has doubled in size. You can no longer delegate merely at the 'task' level; you need to transition to 'strategic' delegation.

options.text: Work twice as many hours to ensure you can still manage the tactical delegation across the larger portfolio.
Delegate entire strategic outcomes (e.g., 'Increase user retention by 5%') to your managers, define the boundary conditions, and empower them to design the tactics to achieve it.
Hire more junior staff to handle the extra tactical work while you continue to manage it all directly.
Assign the strategic outcomes to your managers but demand daily status reports on their tactical execution.

scenario: An empowered team is struggling to make a critical architectural decision because they are stuck in 'analysis paralysis' trying to find the perfect solution.

options.text: Make the decision for them immediately to unblock the work.
Tell them to keep analyzing until they are 100% sure, as architectural decisions are too important to rush.
Facilitate a session to help them define the 'two-way door' (reversible) vs 'one-way door' nature of the decision, and set a hard timebox for them to commit to a path.
Flip a coin in front of them to show that making any decision is better than no decision.

scenario: You need to evaluate a frontline manager's performance for the year. They have excellent individual output, but their team is completely dependent on them and lacks autonomy.

options.text: Give them a top rating because their individual output guarantees high-quality deliverables.
Rate them highly but add a minor note in their review that they should try to delegate more.
Hold them accountable in their review for the lack of team development, emphasizing that a manager's primary success metric is the capability and empowerment of their team, not personal output.
Threaten to put them on a performance improvement plan unless they immediately delegate 50% of their work.

scenario: During a 1-on-1, a usually reliable direct report suddenly breaks down in tears, admitting they are overwhelmed by a recent, severe personal loss.

options.text: Listen actively without interrupting, express genuine condolences, ask how you can best support them right now, and offer immediate time off while you handle their urgent tasks.
Express sympathy, quickly hand them a tissue, and immediately refer them to the company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP) so professionals can handle it.
Tell them to take a deep breath and remind them that keeping personal and professional lives separate can be a good distraction from grief.
Listen patiently, express your condolences, and suggest they take the rest of the day off, but ask them to finalize a pending report before logging off.

scenario: You are under immense pressure from executive leadership. During a team sync, a subordinate asks a repetitive question, and you snap at them in frustration in front of the whole team.

options.text: Pause the meeting immediately, apologize sincerely to the individual and the team for losing your temper, and calmly answer the question.
Send a private message to the individual after the meeting apologizing for your tone, but say nothing to the rest of the team.
Ignore the outburst and move on; as a manager, your team needs to understand that you are under high stress and occasionally lack patience.
At the end of the meeting, briefly state that everyone needs to pay better attention so you don't have to get frustrated.

scenario: A high-performing manager reporting to you has recently become withdrawn, irritable, and cynical during leadership meetings, which is completely out of character.

options.text: Schedule an informal, private check-in, mention the specific changes you've noticed using non-judgmental language, and ask how they are doing and how you can support them.
Assume they are just going through a phase and give them space, hoping they will bounce back on their own.
Formally warn them that their negative attitude is impacting the leadership team and needs to be corrected immediately.
Lighten their workload temporarily without explaining why, assuming burnout is the cause of their irritability.

scenario: The company just announced a massive restructuring. Though your department is safe, your team is highly anxious and distracted by rumors of layoffs.

options.text: Hold a team meeting to acknowledge the fear and uncertainty, validate their feelings, share exactly what you know (and don't know), and maintain an open-door policy.
Tell the team to ignore the rumors and focus strictly on their current KPIs, as worrying won't change anything.
Send an email reassuring them that their jobs are safe and urging them to stay positive and productive.
Join in on the speculation with them to show solidarity and make them feel you are all in the same boat.

scenario: During a performance review, you deliver constructive feedback to an employee. They immediately become defensive, cross their arms, and accuse you of not appreciating their hard work.

options.text: Maintain a calm demeanor, validate their feeling of being unappreciated, pause the feedback, and ask them to share their perspective on their contributions.
Tell them they are being defensive and that they need to learn how to take feedback professionally.
Backtrack on the feedback slightly to de-escalate the situation and preserve the relationship.
Listen to their defense briefly, then redirect them back to the data and metrics that support your original feedback.

scenario: You notice that a neurodivergent team member who prefers written communication is being consistently talked over and ignored by more extroverted peers during brainstorming sessions.

options.text: Tell the employee they need to be more assertive and speak up louder if they want their ideas heard.
Intervene in the moment to create space for them to speak, and later implement inclusive meeting practices like pre-reading materials and written submission options.
Ask the extroverted team members to quiet down and be more respectful.
Meet with the employee privately to collect their ideas and present them on their behalf in the next meeting.

scenario: A direct report confides in you that they are suffering from severe imposter syndrome and feel they don't deserve their recent promotion.

options.text: Listen empathetically, normalize the feeling by sharing a time you felt similarly, and actively point out the specific strengths and successes that earned them the role.
Dismiss their concern kindly by saying 'You're doing great, don't worry about it!' and move on.
Question whether they are truly ready for the role if they are lacking this much confidence.
Provide them with a list of books and podcasts on building self-confidence and check in on their reading progress next week.

scenario: Your team has been working 60-hour weeks to hit a deadline. The CEO just dropped another 'urgent' initiative on your desk, demanding immediate action.

options.text: Push back firmly with the CEO, explaining your team's burnout and negotiating a delayed start date or dropped priority to protect your team's wellbeing.
Pass the project to the team but apologize profusely, telling them you have no power to stop the CEO's requests.
Rally the team with free coffee and pizza, emphasizing that 'we just have to push through this one last time.'
Assign the new work immediately without acknowledging their current workload, as executives expect results, not complaints.

scenario: You have to inform a highly dedicated employee that they did not get the promotion they have been working toward for over a year.

options.text: Send them an email on Friday afternoon so they have the weekend to process the disappointment privately.
Meet with them face-to-face, deliver the news clearly and compassionately, acknowledge their hard work and disappointment, and offer to build a concrete development plan when they are ready.
Blame the decision entirely on upper management or HR so the employee doesn't direct their anger at you.
Deliver the news in person, but immediately pivot to talking about the areas where they failed to meet expectations.

scenario: An employee makes a critical error that costs the company a significant client. They come into your office visibly shaking and panic-stricken to confess the mistake.

options.text: Calm them down, assure them that mistakes happen, and immediately take over the situation to fix it yourself.
Express severe disappointment and remind them of the financial implications of their carelessness.
Focus strictly on the facts of the error, ignoring their emotional state, and demand a written incident report by end of day.
De-escalate their panic first by managing your own reaction, assure them you will solve this together, and collaboratively draft a remediation plan once they are calm.

scenario: You conduct an anonymous team pulse survey, and the results show that your team finds you unapproachable and intimidating.

options.text: Thank the team for the feedback, sincerely reflect on your behavior, and open a dialogue to understand specific actions you can take to foster a safer environment.
Ignore the feedback, assuming that being respected and being liked are two different things and intimidation drives results.
Address it in the next meeting by asking, 'Who said I was intimidating? My door is always open!'
Acknowledge the feedback in an email and make a conscious effort to smile more and say hello in the mornings.

scenario: Two managers who report to you are in a heated conflict over shared resources. Both are emotionally triggered and attacking each other's competence.

options.text: Tell them to figure it out professionally or you will cut both of their resource allocations.
Meet with each separately to let them vent, validate the underlying emotional needs (e.g., feeling unsupported), then facilitate a mediated dialogue focused on shared goals.
Listen to both sides and make an executive decision on the resources yourself to end the arguing.
Put them in a room together and refuse to let them leave until they compromise.

scenario: An employee returns to work after a 3-month medical leave. They seem isolated, hesitant to engage, and overwhelmed by the pace of the team.

options.text: Assume they just need time and treat them exactly like everyone else so they don't feel singled out.
Schedule a warm welcome back 1-on-1, explicitly ask about their current capacity and comfort level, and co-create a gradual ramp-up plan.
Assign them to a high-profile project immediately to show you still believe in their capabilities.
Assign a peer buddy to help them catch up on what they missed, but don't adjust their core deliverables.

scenario: A normally quiet team member finally speaks up with an idea in a meeting, but a more senior team member immediately shoots the idea down in a condescending tone.

options.text: Say nothing in the moment to avoid conflict, but privately encourage the quiet employee later.
Agree with the senior member since their technical expertise is usually right.
Politely interrupt the senior member, validate the quiet employee's courage to share, and guide the team to explore the merits of the idea before dismissing it.
Publicly reprimand the senior member for their tone to ensure everyone knows condescension is unacceptable.

scenario: You are dealing with severe personal issues at home and feel exhausted. A direct report comes to you with a minor, easily solvable complaint, and you feel yourself getting angry.

options.text: Snap at them to solve it themselves because you have bigger problems to deal with.
Suppress your anger, force a smile, and solve the problem for them as quickly as possible so they leave.
Recognize your own emotional state, politely pause the conversation, explain you are currently distracted, and ask if you can reconvene in an hour.
Listen to their complaint but offer very short, blunt answers to show you do not have time for this.

scenario: An employee approaches you, deeply frustrated, stating they end up doing all the 'office housework' (taking notes, scheduling, organizing birthdays) and it is impacting their real work.

options.text: Acknowledge the inequity, validate their frustration, and immediately implement a rotating schedule for all administrative tasks across the entire team.
Tell them they are great at it and the team appreciates it, encouraging them to keep doing it.
Tell them to just stop doing the tasks and let things fall through the cracks until others step up.
Thank them for bringing it up and ask for volunteers in the next team meeting to help them out.

scenario: Your manager openly criticizes your team's recent performance in a cross-departmental meeting. You feel defensive and embarrassed.

options.text: Argue back passionately in the meeting to defend your team's honor.
Remain composed, acknowledge the feedback professionally in the moment, and schedule a private meeting with your manager later to discuss the critique and its delivery.
Stay silent, but complain about your manager to your team afterward to build solidarity.
Accept the criticism silently and immediately forward the harsh feedback to your team to motivate them.

scenario: You have a new hire whose communication style is very direct and blunt due to cultural differences, which is upsetting some of the more relationship-oriented team members.

options.text: Tell the new hire they are being rude and must adopt the team's softer communication style immediately.
Engage the new hire privately to understand their perspective, coach them gently on the team's norms, and educate the broader team on interpreting different cultural communication styles.
Tell the rest of the team they need to stop being so sensitive and focus on the work.
Act as a constant translator between the new hire and the team to prevent any direct conflict.

scenario: An employee confides that they are struggling to pay their rent due to an unexpected medical bill and asks for an off-cycle raise.

options.text: Tell them raises are strictly performance-based and their financial situation is not the company's problem.
Express deep empathy for their situation, explain the constraints around off-cycle raises, and actively help them explore company emergency funds, EAP resources, or overtime opportunities.
Give them a personal loan from your own pocket to solve the immediate crisis.
Promise you will fight for a massive bonus for them at the end of the year to make up for it.

scenario: A well-liked, long-tenured employee was unexpectedly fired for policy violations. The team is shocked, grieving, and demanding answers you legally cannot give.

options.text: Refuse to discuss the matter entirely, citing HR confidentiality, and tell everyone to get back to work.
Hold a team meeting to acknowledge the emotional impact of the sudden departure, validate their feelings of shock, clearly state the limits of what you can share, and focus on supporting each other.
Share the confidential reasons for the firing off-the-record so the team understands and moves on.
Focus only on redistributing the fired employee's workload and downplay the emotional impact.

scenario: You have a highly anxious direct report who constantly asks for reassurance on minor tasks, taking up a significant amount of your time.

options.text: Ignore their messages to force them to become self-reliant.
Recognize the underlying anxiety, patiently validate their competence, and work together to establish check-in boundaries (e.g., reviewing tasks once daily) to build their confidence gradually.
Continue providing constant reassurance, sacrificing your own time to keep them calm.
Tell them bluntly that they are being needy and need to trust themselves more.

scenario: A pregnant employee on your team expresses deep anxiety that taking maternity leave will derail her chances of being promoted to a senior role next year.

options.text: Tell her that taking time off obviously impacts output, so she should lower her expectations for a promotion.
Validate her concerns, actively reaffirm her value to the team, and collaboratively build a career progression plan that accounts for her leave and ensures her trajectory remains intact.
Promise her the promotion immediately so she doesn't have to worry during her leave.
Reassure her with platitudes like 'family comes first' without discussing any concrete career plans.

scenario: During a contentious strategy debate, a peer manager becomes highly emotional and accuses your team of actively sabotaging their metrics.

options.text: Yell back, aggressively defending your team and listing the peer's own failures.
Manage your own defensive trigger, pause, acknowledge their frustration without accepting blame, and suggest taking a 10-minute break before reviewing the data objectively.
Walk out of the room silently to show you won't tolerate being spoken to that way.
Tell them to calm down and stop being so emotional.

scenario: You realize you have developed a strong, unconscious personal dislike for a new team member because they remind you of a difficult former colleague.

options.text: Find reasons to discipline them or manage them out of the team to remove the stress from your life.
Acknowledge this bias to yourself, actively self-monitor your interactions to ensure fairness, and intentionally seek out their positive contributions to reframe your perspective.
Keep your distance from the employee as much as possible to avoid any biased interactions.
Confess your bias to the employee and ask them to bear with you while you work through it.

scenario: A team member shares that their beloved pet of 15 years has just passed away and they are struggling to concentrate.

options.text: Remind them that the bereavement policy only applies to human relatives and they need to work.
Express sincere empathy, validate the depth of the loss, and offer them the day off or lighter duties without requiring them to use formal PTO if possible.
Say 'I'm sorry, it's just a pet, you'll feel better soon' and ask them to finish their current task.
Send them a sympathy card but do not adjust their workload or offer any time off.

scenario: You notice one of your managers uses a very command-and-control style. They get results, but their team's engagement scores have plummeted.

options.text: Praise the manager for getting results and tell the team to stop complaining.
Initiate a coaching conversation focused on empathy and emotional intelligence, tying their long-term success and retention rates to how they make their team feel.
Fire the manager immediately for having low engagement scores.
Send the manager to a mandatory leadership training seminar without discussing the 'why'.

scenario: A direct report who is incredibly enthusiastic and eager to please lacks self-awareness, frequently talking over others and dominating team meetings.

options.text: Shut them down publicly in the next meeting to teach them a lesson about dominating the floor.
Pull them aside privately, validate their passion and good intentions, but provide specific, constructive feedback on how their behavior impacts others and coach them on active listening.
Let them keep dominating because their enthusiasm is good for team energy.
Ask other team members to gently interrupt them when they talk too much.

scenario: You discover that a major promise you made to your team regarding a year-end bonus has been vetoed by the CFO at the last minute.

options.text: Hide the news for as long as possible and hope they forget about the bonus.
Gather the team immediately, own the mistake of promising prematurely, express your genuine shared frustration, explain the business reality transparently, and apologize sincerely.
Tell them the CFO cancelled it and encourage them to complain to finance.
Send a brief email stating that bonuses are cancelled due to budget cuts without further explanation.

scenario: Your team is divided over a sensitive social/political issue that was brought up in the team chat, leading to tension and passive-aggressive behavior.

options.text: Take a side based on your personal beliefs and tell the other side to stop arguing.
Address the tension empathetically, remind the team of core values regarding respect and inclusion, and redirect the focus back to shared goals while offering 1-on-1s for anyone feeling distressed.
Ban all non-work talk completely and threaten disciplinary action for anyone who mentions the issue.
Ignore the tension and hope it blows over in a few days.

scenario: You have to enforce a controversial 'Return to Office' mandate. You personally disagree with it, and you know your team will be furious.

options.text: Tell your team that upper management is making a terrible decision, but you all have to suffer through it.

Acknowledge their frustration and validate the disruption it causes, clearly explain the corporate rationale without throwing leadership under the bus, and focus on providing flexibility where you can.
Enforce the mandate coldly, refusing to entertain any complaints or expressions of frustration.
Pretend you love the new policy and try to convince them it is actually a great idea.

scenario: A chronically negative employee constantly complains about company leadership during team meetings, draining the energy of the rest of the group.

options.text: Agree with their complaints in the meeting to show you are a relatable manager.
Meet with them privately to understand the root cause of their dissatisfaction, validate their feelings, but set a firm boundary that public complaints must be accompanied by constructive solutions.
Fire them immediately for having a bad attitude and ruining team culture.
Interrupt them every time they complain and forcefully change the subject.

scenario: A high-potential employee is dealing with a messy public divorce. They are missing deadlines and their work quality has dropped significantly.

options.text: Put them on a formal Performance Improvement Plan immediately to document the drop in quality.
Approach them with compassion, express concern for their wellbeing, temporarily adjust their workload or deadlines, and ensure they have access to support resources.
Tell them they need to compartmentalize better and leave their personal life at the door.
Quietly reassign their work to other team members without telling them, to avoid adding to their stress.

scenario: You are mediating a conflict between a direct report and a client. The client is being unreasonable and slightly abusive, bringing your employee to tears.

options.text: Side with the client immediately because 'the customer is always right', and reprimand your employee later.
Intervene calmly but firmly to de-escalate, end the meeting to protect your employee, validate the employee's distress afterward, and address the behavior with the client offline.
Stay silent during the meeting, but comfort your employee profusely once the client hangs up.
Yell at the client for making your employee cry and terminate the contract on the spot.

scenario: Two frontline managers reporting to you are locked in a bitter dispute over which of their teams should take ownership of a high-visibility, high-stakes new project.

options.text: Bring both managers together, facilitate a discussion focused on their respective team capacities and strategic alignments, and guide them to a consensus or co-ownership model.
Make the decision yourself immediately based on your gut feeling to stop the arguing and get the project started.
Give the project to a third, less qualified manager just to punish the two fighting managers.
Ask them to submit written proposals defending why their team should get it, and choose the best one.

scenario: A cross-functional peer manager continually publicly blames your team for project delays, even though the delays are caused by their team providing requirements late.

options.text: Schedule a private 1-on-1 with the peer, present objective timeline data neutrally, and collaboratively map out a process to ensure requirements are delivered on time moving forward.
Defend your team publicly in the next meeting by aggressively pointing out exactly when their team delivered the late requirements.
Instruct your team to stop working on the peer's projects altogether until they apologize.
Escalate the issue to your director, providing the timeline data and asking them to talk to the peer's director.

scenario: Two senior individual contributors on your team have a fundamentally different approach to a technical problem, and their debates in team meetings are escalating into personal attacks.

options.text: Intervene immediately when attacks get personal, then set up a structured evaluation session where both approaches are tested against objective project criteria to decide the best path.
Tell them both to act like professionals and figure it out on their own outside of team meetings.
Fire the one who is being more aggressive to set an example for the rest of the team.
Assign them to different projects so they no longer have to interact or debate.

scenario: A key stakeholder is furious because a feature they requested was deprioritized by your product team without their explicit consent.

options.text: Acknowledge their frustration, transparently explain the resource constraints that drove the decision, and collaborate on a revised timeline to deliver the feature.
Apologize profusely and order your team to work overtime to build the feature immediately to appease the stakeholder.
Tell the stakeholder that you are the manager and you decide the priorities, so they need to accept it.
Offer a compromise by delivering a scaled-down, basic version of the feature in the current sprint.

scenario: You oversee two teams that have a historically toxic rivalry. They are now required to merge into a single unit under your leadership.

options.text: Host a transition workshop to explicitly address past frictions, establish new shared goals, and collaboratively define new cultural norms and operational workflows.
Ignore the past rivalry and simply announce the new team structure, expecting everyone to be professional.
Tell everyone that anyone caught participating in the old rivalry will be immediately terminated.
Keep the two teams functionally separate but working under the same umbrella name to minimize immediate friction.

scenario: A newly hired manager on your team wants to completely overhaul a core process, causing deep resentment and resistance from the veteran team members who built it.

options.text: Mediate a session where the new manager presents the benefits of the change and the veterans share their historical context, working together to iterate a hybrid process.
Back the new manager completely and tell the veterans they must adapt to change or leave.
Tell the new manager to abandon their ideas and conform to how the team has always done things to keep the peace.
Allow the new manager to pilot the process with a small subset of the team to prove its value before a full rollout.

scenario: You are cc'd on an email thread between two of your direct reports that has quickly escalated into passive-aggressive, highly defensive territory.

options.text: Reply to both privately asking them to step away from their keyboards, and schedule a brief video call to de-escalate and align them verbally.
Reply-all to the thread telling them both to calm down and stop arguing over email.
Ignore the thread entirely; they are adults and should manage their own inbox conflicts.
Call the instigator of the passive-aggressive tone and tell them to apologize and clarify their intent.

scenario: A critical vendor has failed to meet their SLA for the third time this month. When you confront their account manager, they blame your team's complex requirements.

options.text: Remain objective, review the documented requirements and SLA metrics together, and demand a specific, jointly agreed-upon remediation plan rather than engaging in the blame game.
Accept their excuse temporarily to keep the relationship intact, but privately tell your team to simplify their requests.
Yell at the account manager and immediately terminate the contract, despite the disruption it will cause.
Escalate to the vendor's VP to formally complain about the account manager's lack of accountability.

scenario: During a performance review, an employee strongly disagrees with a 'Needs Improvement' rating, claiming you are biased against them.

options.text: De-escalate by staying calm, validate that reviews can be stressful, and walk through the specific, objective data and examples that led to the rating.
End the meeting immediately and tell them to contact HR if they have a problem with your judgment.
Change the rating to 'Meets Expectations' to avoid the conflict and keep the employee happy.
Listen to their grievances, take notes, and promise to review the data again before finalizing the document.

scenario: Your department is split down the middle regarding a controversial new 'Return to Office' mandate, leading to friction and cliques forming based on their stance.

options.text: Host an open forum to acknowledge the divide, allow people to express their concerns constructively, and pivot the focus to establishing inclusive norms regardless of work location.
Send a memo telling everyone to stop discussing the policy and focus on their work.
Take the side of the pro-office group and marginalize the remote group to force compliance.
Address the cliques directly in 1-on-1s and ask individuals to make an effort to collaborate across the divide.

scenario: An employee complains that their peer is stealing credit for their ideas in meetings with upper management.

options.text: Investigate by speaking to both parties separately, and if true, establish clear attribution norms in meetings and coach the offending employee on collaboration ethics.
Tell the complaining employee they need to speak up louder in meetings if they want credit.
Publicly embarrass the credit-stealing employee in the next management meeting by calling them a liar.
Mediate a meeting between the two of them to clear the air and request they co-present their ideas moving forward.

scenario: Your boss gives you a directive that directly contradicts a compliance policy heavily enforced by the legal department.

options.text: Present your boss with the specific compliance risk, explicitly state your hesitation, and offer to facilitate a meeting with legal to find a compliant alternative.
Follow your boss's directive since they are your direct superior and assume they will take the blame if caught.
Report your boss to the compliance hotline immediately without discussing it with them first.
Refuse to do the task and tell your boss to put the request in writing so you have a paper trail.

scenario: Two team members have a fundamental personality clash; they are both highly effective but cannot spend 5 minutes in a room without arguing over minor details.

options.text: Sit them down to establish strict, professional rules of engagement, focus their interactions solely on task handoffs, and clarify that professional respect is non-negotiable.
Let them argue, assuming that friction produces better ideas and keeps them competitive.
Force them to go to a social lunch together to bond and become friends.
Restructure their workflows so they operate entirely in silos and never have to interact.

scenario: A subordinate bypasses you entirely and goes to your director to complain about a decision you made regarding project timelines.

options.text: Schedule a 1-on-1 with the subordinate to understand their frustration, explain why the decision was made, and firmly reinforce the expectation of coming to you first in the future.
Complain to your director about the subordinate's insubordination and ask the director to scold them.
Retaliate by giving the subordinate the worst tasks on the project to teach them a lesson.
Address it openly in the next team meeting, stating that the chain of command must be respected.

scenario: Your team's budget was slashed by 20%, causing intense conflict among your direct reports over whose projects will lose funding.

options.text: Lead a transparent prioritization exercise based on department OKRs, requiring the team to objectively rank projects by ROI and strategic impact to distribute the cuts fairly.
Cut the budgets of the managers who argue the least, as they are the easiest to manage.
Tell them to fight it out among themselves and bring you a finalized budget by the end of the week.
Apply a flat 20% cut across all projects equally, regardless of the strategic impact, to seem fair.

scenario: The sales team sold a customized feature to a major client that your engineering team says is impossible to build within the promised timeframe.

options.text: Facilitate a sync between the sales lead and engineering lead to understand the client's core need, and negotiate a phased delivery or alternative solution that engineering can actually build.
Tell the engineering team they just have to figure it out because the company cannot lose the client.
Call the client directly and tell them the sales team lied to them and you cannot deliver it.
Escalate to the executive team immediately to mediate the dispute between sales and engineering.

scenario: A highly productive but arrogant team member refuses to follow newly established compliance protocols, stating they slow down their work.

options.text: Have a direct conversation explaining that compliance is a non-negotiable part of performance, and formally document the warning while offering to help streamline their workflow.
Look the other way because they are a top performer and their output is too valuable to risk.
Suspend them immediately without warning to prove that you are serious about compliance.
Ask a junior team member to quietly do the compliance paperwork for the top performer.

scenario: A dispute arises between a manager on your team and a human resources representative over a candidate the manager wants to hire, who HR claims fails a background requirement.

options.text: Meet with the HR rep to fully understand the specific policy and risks, then sit down with your manager to explore alternative candidates or proper exception protocols if applicable.
Side blindly with your manager and write an angry email to the HR director accusing them of blocking talent.
Fire the candidate immediately and reprimand the manager for questioning HR.
Advise your manager to drop it, as fighting with HR is a battle that can never be won.

scenario: Your team feels completely overwhelmed and is directing their anger at you, claiming you over-promised deliverables to senior leadership.

options.text: Acknowledge their frustration without getting defensive, review the commitments together to identify scope that can be trimmed, and promise to push back on leadership.
Defend your decisions by explaining that senior leadership forced your hand and you had no choice.
Tell the team they are being lazy and need to step up if they want to succeed in this company.
Apologize profusely and take on a massive amount of the tactical work yourself to ease their burden.

scenario: An internal client is demanding that your team drop all current work to handle their 'emergency' request, causing a severe conflict over priorities.

options.text: Implement an objective intake process, assess the true business impact of the 'emergency' against current work, and transparently communicate the trade-offs to the client.
Accept the emergency request to avoid conflict, and tell your team to work late to catch up on the rest.
Ignore the client's emails and phone calls until you finish your current sprint.
Tell the client you can only give them 20% of your team's time and they will just have to deal with a slower delivery.

scenario: Two members of your team are constantly bickering over the thermostat and office noise levels, creating an uncomfortable environment for everyone else.

options.text: Bring them together to mutually agree on a compromise (e.g., specific quiet hours, use of headphones, and a set temperature range) and enforce it consistently.
Send a mass email to the whole team reminding everyone to be considerate of others in the office.
Threaten to revoke both of their in-office privileges if they don't stop acting like children.
Move their desks to opposite sides of the building so they don't interact anymore.

scenario: A conflict arises when a remote worker feels that the in-office workers are intentionally leaving them out of impromptu decision-making meetings.

options.text: Validate the remote worker's concern, and establish a strict team norm that all decisions must be documented and finalized in hybrid-friendly forums.
Tell the remote worker that missing out on impromptu meetings is just the price they pay for the luxury of working from home.
Ban all in-office impromptu conversations to ensure total equality.
Ask the in-office team to try to remember to call the remote worker if something important comes up.

scenario: You inherit a team where a clique of senior employees routinely bullies new hires by withholding information and setting them up to fail.

options.text: Address the behavior immediately in individual meetings, set strict consequences for retaliation, and implement a transparent, documented onboarding process that bypasses the clique.
Try to win over the clique's leadership by being friendly, hoping they will naturally soften their behavior toward new hires.
Fire the entire clique immediately without due process.
Warn new hires during the interview process that the culture is tough and they need thick skin.

scenario: A dispute occurs between your department and the marketing team over the messaging in a new campaign, which you believe makes promises your operations team cannot fulfill.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the marketing director, present operational capacity data calmly, and collaboratively draft revised messaging that protects the brand and operations.
Let marketing run the campaign; it's their job to sell, and your team will just have to handle the customer complaints later.
Send a company-wide email denouncing the marketing campaign as a lie.
Escalate to the CEO and demand that they force marketing to pull the campaign.

scenario: An employee feels they were unfairly passed over for a leadership role that went to an external hire, and they are now being overtly hostile to the new leader.

options.text: Meet with the employee to acknowledge their disappointment, firmly set boundaries against hostile behavior, and offer to build a development plan for future opportunities.
Ignore the hostility, assuming the employee will eventually get over their disappointment.
Tell the employee they are acting unprofessionally and demote them to teach them a lesson.
Advise the new external hire to tread lightly and try to appease the hostile employee.

scenario: Your team is executing a project for a client who keeps moving the goalposts, leading to a breakdown in relations between the client and your project manager.
