options.text: Step in as a sponsor, organize a reset meeting with the client to firmly re-establish the original statement of work, and implement a strict change-order process.
Tell your project manager to just do whatever the client wants to keep them happy.
Cancel the project and fire the client for being too difficult.
Replace the project manager with someone else, hoping a new personality will fix the client's behavior.

scenario: A rumor is circulating that one of your team members is going to be fired. The team member is panicked, and the rest of the team is distracted and gossiping.

options.text: Meet with the affected employee to assure them of their standing, then address the team to firmly shut down the rumor mill and reiterate the importance of professionalism.
Ignore the rumor; addressing it will only make it seem more legitimate.
Try to figure out who started the rumor and publicly shame them in front of the department.
Send a cryptic email saying 'don't believe everything you hear' and leave it at that.

scenario: You discover that a conflict between two of your direct reports stems from a cultural misunderstanding regarding directness and feedback styles.

options.text: Facilitate a respectful dialogue where both parties share their cultural perspectives on communication, and help them establish a mutually agreeable framework for future feedback.
Tell the more direct employee to soften their tone, as it is always better to be polite in the workplace.
Tell the offended employee to stop being so sensitive and adapt to the local corporate culture.
Send them both a link to a corporate training video on cultural sensitivity and tell them to figure it out.

scenario: A union representative approaches you with a grievance, claiming a new scheduling policy you implemented violates the collective bargaining agreement.

options.text: Suspend the policy temporarily, review the collective bargaining agreement with HR/Labor Relations, and schedule a formal meeting with the union rep to resolve the discrepancy.
Argue with the union representative that the policy is necessary for business efficiency and refuse to change it.
Ignore the grievance entirely and continue enforcing the scheduling policy.
Tell the union representative you will look into it, but delay taking any action for several weeks.

scenario: A highly creative employee and a highly analytical employee are clashing on a joint project, constantly dismissing each other's contributions as either 'unrealistic' or 'boring'.

options.text: Mediate a session to highlight how their diverse strengths complement each other, and help them divide the project phases so both can lead in their respective areas of expertise.
Tell them to compromise by meeting in the middle, resulting in a mediocre output that pleases neither.
Force the creative employee to follow the analytical employee's lead, as data always wins.
Have them work separately on two different versions of the project and you pick the winner at the end.

scenario: You have a matrix management structure, and one of your reports is receiving completely contradictory instructions from you and their functional project manager.

options.text: Set up a meeting with the functional project manager to align your expectations, prioritize the employee's workload together, and present a unified front moving forward.
Tell the employee to prioritize your instructions because you write their performance review.
Tell the employee it's their job to figure out how to satisfy both of you.
Email the functional manager and tell them to back off and stop interfering with your report.

scenario: During a crisis, a senior engineer strongly advocates for a risky hotfix, while the QA lead aggressively demands a full regression test that will take 24 hours.

options.text: Facilitate a rapid risk-assessment discussion focusing on business impact versus technical risk, guide them to a data-driven decision, and take ultimate accountability for the call.
Side with the senior engineer immediately to fix the issue faster and appease stakeholders.
Refuse to make a decision and let them fight until one gives up.
Mandate a compromised 12-hour testing window, regardless of whether it actually covers the necessary technical checks.

scenario: An employee complains that you are micromanaging them and it is causing tension between you two. They request that you back off entirely.

options.text: Listen openly without getting defensive, discuss their need for autonomy versus your need for visibility, and agree on a structured reporting cadence that satisfies both.
Tell them you wouldn't have to micromanage if they were better at their job.
Back off entirely as requested to avoid the conflict, risking project failure.
Acknowledge their feeling but explain that your management style is just naturally hands-on and they need to adjust.

scenario: You are reviewing end-of-month performance metrics and notice a significant discrepancy between the data reported by your internal CRM and the data from the finance department.

options.text: Initiate a cross-functional root-cause analysis with finance and IT to map data flows, identify the point of divergence, and establish a single source of truth.
Report the CRM numbers to your leadership, as those are the metrics your team is officially measured against.
Ignore the discrepancy, assuming finance will eventually catch and correct any accounting errors on their end.
Ask an analyst on your team to manually reconcile the two reports for this month so you can submit your update on time.

scenario: Midway through Q3, executive leadership announces an immediate 15% budget cut across all departments due to a market downturn.

options.text: Apply a flat 15% cut across all your team's projects and software tools to ensure everyone shares the burden equally.
Evaluate all current initiatives against the company's core strategic priorities, and pause or cut the lowest-ROI projects entirely to protect high-impact work.
Refuse to cut the budget, arguing to leadership that your department's work is too critical to be compromised.
Ask your team for voluntary ideas on how to save money and implement whatever they suggest.

scenario: A critical third-party software vendor that your operations rely on suddenly goes bankrupt, and their services will shut down in 48 hours.

options.text: Panic and immediately demand that your engineering team build a custom replacement overnight.
Form a rapid-response task force to assess the immediate operational impact, deploy manual workarounds for critical flows, and simultaneously begin evaluating emergency alternative vendors.
Wait to see if another company acquires the vendor at the last minute to avoid unnecessary disruption.
Notify stakeholders of the impending outage and ask for an extension on all current deadlines until a solution is found.

scenario: You have two high-priority projects assigned to your team, but due to unexpected absences, you only have the bandwidth to successfully deliver one on time.

options.text: Force your team to work massive overtime to deliver both, as mid-level managers must find ways to meet all executive demands.
Analyze the business impact and strategic alignment of both projects, make a data-driven recommendation on which to prioritize, and escalate to your director for final alignment.
Split the team's focus equally between both projects, accepting that both will be delivered late or with lower quality.
Pick the project that is easiest to complete quickly so you can at least secure one 'win' for the team.

scenario: A new process rollout designed to increase efficiency is actually causing massive bottlenecks and frustrating your team. The rollout was your idea.

options.text: Double down on the rollout, insisting that the team just needs more time to overcome the learning curve.
Acknowledge the issues, temporarily pause the new process, solicit direct feedback from the end-users to identify the friction points, and iterate on the design.
Abandon the new process entirely and silently revert to the old way to stop the complaints.
Keep the process but assign a dedicated troubleshooter to help people navigate the bottlenecks.

scenario: You identify a systemic flaw in a legacy workflow that involves three different departments. Fixing it requires significant upfront effort but will save hundreds of hours annually.

options.text: Ignore it, as overhauling cross-departmental legacy processes is too politically risky and resource-intensive.
Map the current vs. future state, calculate the ROI, build a business case, and present it to the other department heads to secure buy-in for a joint improvement initiative.
Fix only the parts of the workflow that touch your department, leaving the rest broken.
Complain to executive leadership that the other departments are using an inefficient process and demand they fix it.

scenario: Executive leadership demands a product launch by a specific date. After analyzing the requirements, your technical leads prove mathematically that the date is impossible without severe quality compromises.

options.text: Agree to the date anyway, hoping the team can somehow pull off a miracle if pushed hard enough.
Present leadership with a transparent trade-off matrix: offer to meet the date with a reduced feature set (MVP), or deliver the full scope on a realistic, revised timeline.
Tell leadership flatly that the date is impossible and wait for them to suggest a new one.
Accept the date but heavily compromise quality, assuming you can patch the product after launch.

scenario: Your department's output has mysteriously dropped by 20% over the last month. There have been no changes to staffing, tools, or major projects.

options.text: Send a stern email reminding everyone of their KPIs and warning that underperformance will not be tolerated.
Conduct a deep-dive investigation by analyzing operational metrics for bottlenecks and holding open 1-on-1s to uncover hidden cultural or process friction.
Assume it is just seasonal fatigue and wait another month to see if metrics bounce back.
Implement a new daily status report to track exactly what everyone is doing hour-by-hour.

scenario: You need to purchase a new tool for your team. Option A is expensive but fully customized. Option B is cheap, off-the-shelf, and meets 80% of your needs.

options.text: Always buy the cheapest option to save department budget, regardless of the manual workarounds required.
Always buy the premium option, as having the best tools guarantees the best performance.
Conduct a cost-benefit analysis comparing the price difference against the labor cost of the workarounds for Option B, making a decision based on long-term ROI.
Let your frontline team vote on which tool they want and go with the majority.

scenario: A highly specialized, critical team member abruptly resigns three weeks before a major deliverable is due, leaving a massive knowledge gap.

options.text: Panic and tell stakeholders the project is cancelled due to unforeseen circumstances.
Immediately assess the remaining critical-path tasks, redistribute them among the remaining team members based on adjacent skills, and transparently notify stakeholders of potential minor delays.
Demand the resigning employee stay until the project is finished, threatening to give a bad reference if they leave.
Hire an expensive emergency contractor without checking the budget to ensure the deadline is met.

scenario: While conducting a routine audit, you discover that your team has inadvertently been violating a minor industry compliance regulation for the past six months.

options.text: Quietly fix the process moving forward but do not report the past violations to avoid getting your team in trouble.
Immediately report the finding to the compliance/legal team, presenting a clear summary of the scope of the error and a finalized remediation plan to ensure it never happens again.
Blame the previous manager who originally set up the process to protect your own reputation.
Stop all department work immediately until a full external audit can be conducted.

scenario: Your team is constantly dealing with a recurring bug in your internal system. They apply a quick patch every week, but it always breaks again.

options.text: Continue applying the weekly patch because dedicating time to a full rewrite would hurt your short-term velocity metrics.
Formally allocate capacity in the next sprint specifically for addressing technical debt, requiring the team to identify and solve the root cause permanently.
Tell the team they are incompetent for not fixing it properly the first time.
Submit a ticket to IT to fix it, and just wait indefinitely for them to get around to it.

scenario: You need to decide whether to build a custom internal reporting application or purchase a SaaS subscription that does essentially the same thing.

options.text: Build it internally because engineering teams always prefer building custom solutions over using third-party tools.
Evaluate the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) including maintenance, time-to-market, and whether this tool represents a core competitive advantage, before making a decision.
Buy the SaaS product immediately because building internal tools is always a distraction.
Start building it internally, and if it gets too difficult, switch to buying the SaaS product later.

scenario: A major shift in the macroeconomic environment suddenly makes the strategic roadmap you spent three months building completely obsolete.

options.text: Stick to the original roadmap because you already invested so much time and effort into planning it.
Acknowledge the sunk cost, rapidly gather market data to reassess priorities, and pivot the team to a new, relevant strategy while clearly explaining the 'why' behind the change.
Wait for executive leadership to tell you exactly what to do next.
Make incremental tweaks to the old roadmap so it looks slightly updated, avoiding a full disruption.

scenario: A highly capable direct report comes to you with a complex operational problem, clearly expecting you to give them the answer.

options.text: Solve the problem for them immediately so they can get back to work quickly.
Refuse to help and tell them to figure it out themselves because that is what they are paid to do.
Resist giving the answer; instead, use coaching questions to guide them through analyzing the root cause and evaluating potential solutions themselves.
Give them a few hints and tell them to come back when they have the final answer.

scenario: You must make a technical decision, but your two best Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) are giving you completely contradictory advice.

options.text: Side with the SME who has been at the company the longest.
Facilitate a joint session where both SMEs map their proposals against a shared set of objective business criteria (e.g., cost, scalability, risk) to uncover the best hybrid or objective path.
Flip a coin or choose blindly, as both options are probably fine if the experts are split.
Hire an external consultant to break the tie.

scenario: Your team is 90% finished with a major feature when new user research reveals that the feature will not actually solve the customer's core problem.

options.text: Launch it anyway to hit the quarterly goal, as sunk costs dictate you must finish what you start.
Immediately halt development, present the data to stakeholders, acknowledge the sunk cost, and propose a pivot to a solution that actually delivers customer value.
Finish the feature but quietly bury it so no one realizes it doesn't work.
Launch it, but immediately start building a 'version 2' to fix the fundamental flaws.

scenario: An experimental pilot initiative you championed is clearly failing, missing all success metrics and bleeding resources.

options.text: Pour more resources into it, convinced that it just needs a little more funding to succeed.
Conduct an objective post-mortem, formally kill the project to cut losses, and share the learnings transparently with leadership to ensure the failure provides institutional value.
Hide the negative metrics and report that the project is 'still gathering data'.
Quietly wind the project down over several months so no one notices the failure.

scenario: Your department is caught in a cycle of constant 'firefighting', dealing with urgent daily crises that prevent them from executing proactive, strategic work.

options.text: Praise the team for their heroism and firefighting skills to keep morale high.
Mandate that they ignore the fires and strictly focus on strategic work, letting the daily crises burn.
Analyze incident logs to identify the root causes of the recurring 'fires', and reallocate a percentage of team capacity specifically to building systemic, preventative fixes.
Ask leadership for more headcount so you have dedicated people just for firefighting.

scenario: You need to make a critical market-entry decision within 24 hours, but you only have about 50% of the data you would normally want.

options.text: Refuse to make the decision until you have 100% of the data, even if it means missing the market window.
Make the decision using the available data and reasonable assumptions, explicitly state the known risks, and establish rapid feedback loops to course-correct quickly if needed.
Make a random guess, as agonizing over incomplete data is a waste of time.
Delay the decision by a week, hoping more data organically surfaces.

scenario: A key competitor unexpectedly launches a disruptive new feature. Your sales team is panicking and demanding your team build a copycat feature immediately.

options.text: Drop everything and build the copycat feature to calm the sales team down.
Objectively assess the threat level, consult product data and customer feedback to determine if it aligns with your strategy, and present a measured, strategic response to leadership.
Ignore the competitor entirely, as focusing on competitors distracts from your own vision.
Tell sales you will add it to the backlog and eventually get to it next year.

scenario: A standard operational process requires approvals from five different managers, creating a massive bottleneck that delays client deliverables.

options.text: Yell at the other managers to review the approvals faster.
Map the risk profile of the approvals, propose an updated RACI matrix that empowers frontline staff to auto-approve low-risk items, and seek consensus to streamline the workflow.
Bypass the approval process entirely to get the client deliverables out on time.
Set up an automated email reminder that pesters the managers until they approve the items.

scenario: The CEO suggests a highly specific, tactical solution to a problem in your department. Based on your technical expertise, you know for a fact their solution will break the system.

options.text: Implement the CEO's solution exactly as asked; if it breaks, it is their fault.
Acknowledge their underlying goal, respectfully present data demonstrating why the specific tactic carries high risk, and propose a safer, more effective alternative to achieve their goal.
Ignore the CEO's suggestion and implement your own solution without telling them.
Implement a scaled-down version of the CEO's idea to appease them, even if it causes minor issues.

scenario: Your entire department is slowed down because a critical process relies on a single employee who is the only one who knows how to use a legacy database (a single point of failure).

options.text: Keep giving them the work because they are the fastest at it, maximizing short-term efficiency.
Immediately mandate that they stop all routine work to write documentation and cross-train two peers, accepting the short-term slowdown to eliminate the systemic risk.
Threaten to fire them if they don't share their knowledge, assuming they are hoarding it for job security.
Ask them to document the process in their free time outside of standard working hours.

scenario: You realize that one of your department's primary OKRs (e.g., speed of delivery) is in direct, systemic conflict with another department's OKRs (e.g., quality assurance).

options.text: Fight aggressively to ensure your department hits its OKRs, letting the other department worry about their own problems.
Initiate a meeting with the peer manager to elevate the view to company-wide strategic goals, and collaboratively negotiate a balanced SLA that optimizes for the overall business.
Slow your team down to help them meet their quality goals, sacrificing your own review metrics entirely.
Escalate to the VP level immediately, complaining that the company goals are poorly designed.

scenario: You ran a limited pilot for a new operational workflow. The top-line metric looks great, but secondary metrics indicate employee burnout might be increasing.

options.text: Roll out the workflow company-wide immediately because the top-line metric is all executive leadership cares about.
Deep-dive into the secondary metrics, conduct qualitative interviews to understand the burnout drivers, and iterate the workflow design before deciding whether to scale.
Kill the project entirely because any sign of burnout is unacceptable.
Roll it out but tell the team they need to practice better self-care to manage the stress.

scenario: Your department is tasked with reducing operational costs by 10% next year, but you cannot reduce headcount or compromise output quality.

options.text: Cut all training, travel, and team-building budgets to zero, regardless of the impact on culture.
Conduct a bottom-up process audit with your team to identify waste, renegotiate vendor contracts, and automate repetitive tasks to achieve sustainable efficiency gains.
Tell leadership the goal is mathematically impossible without cutting headcount.
Implement strict micromanagement policies to ensure nobody wastes a single minute of company time.

scenario: A massive enterprise client requests a bespoke feature that deviates entirely from your product roadmap, threatening to churn if you don't build it.

options.text: Build it immediately because retaining massive clients is always the top priority.

Evaluate the business value of the client against the opportunity cost of derailing the roadmap, assess if the feature has broader market appeal, and make a strategic recommendation to the executive team.
Refuse the client bluntly, stating you never deviate from the roadmap.
Agree to build it but place it at the very bottom of the backlog, hoping they forget about it.

scenario: You inherit a team managing a complex, undocumented legacy system. It is currently stable, but nobody truly understands how it works.

options.text: Leave it alone; 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it.'
Prioritize a dedicated 'discovery' phase to map the architecture, write robust documentation, and assess the risk of modernization versus maintaining the status quo.
Immediately mandate that the team rewrite the entire system in modern code, regardless of the disruption.
Hire an external consultant to look at it, but don't dedicate any internal team time to it.

scenario: There is massive hype around a new Generative AI tool. Leadership wants you to roll it out to your department immediately to 'increase productivity.'

options.text: Mandate immediate adoption for all team members and tell them to figure out how to use it.
Design a controlled, measurable pilot with a small group of power users, establish clear ROI and security criteria, and use the results to build a strategic rollout and training plan.
Push back on leadership, stating that AI is a fad and poses too many security risks to use.
Buy the licenses but leave it up to individual team members whether they want to use it or not.

scenario: A sudden, unpredictable external event (e.g., a global supply chain strike) immediately halts progress on your department's most critical quarterly initiative.

options.text: Do nothing and tell leadership you are waiting for the external event to resolve itself.
Rapidly assess the blast radius, activate contingency plans or alternative sourcing, communicate revised timelines to stakeholders, and temporarily reallocate team capacity to secondary goals.
Blame the supply chain team for not predicting the unpredictable event.
Ask the team to work on the project anyway, even if they can't make actual progress.

scenario: Your team spends 20 hours a week manually compiling a report for senior leadership. Automating it would take 80 hours of engineering time upfront.

options.text: Continue doing it manually because you cannot spare 80 hours of engineering time right now.
Build a business case demonstrating the 4-week ROI payback period, and explicitly carve out the 80 hours in the next sprint to automate the task permanently.
Tell leadership you are no longer going to provide the report because it takes too much time.
Ask a junior employee to try automating it in their spare time between other tasks.

scenario: You made a strategic decision last quarter to adopt a new framework. It is now clear that the decision was wrong, and the framework is severely holding the team back.

options.text: Hide the data showing the framework is failing to protect your professional reputation.
Own the mistake transparently with your team and leadership, conduct a blameless post-mortem to learn from the error, and swiftly pivot to a better solution.
Blame the team for not implementing the framework correctly.
Quietly phase the framework out over the next year so nobody notices the mistake.

scenario: Your organization introduces a sweeping new enterprise management system that replaces a tool your team has used for over five years. Several team members actively resist the shift, complaining about lost productivity during sprint planning.

options.text: Acknowledge their frustration with the transition, clearly communicate the long-term strategic reasons for the change, and provide targeted training resources while setting firm expectations for adoption.
Inform the team that executive leadership mandated the software and that non-compliance will directly affect their performance ratings.
Allow resistant team members to continue using the legacy tool for daily tasks while officially logging updates into the new system yourself.
Extend current sprint deadlines significantly and reduce output targets until the team naturally gets comfortable with the new tool over time.

scenario: Midway through executing a major project, senior executives announce a strategic pivot due to shifting market conditions, rendering three weeks of your team's completed work redundant.

options.text: Complain to your direct reports about upper management's lack of vision to build camaraderie and show that you share their frustration.
Host a team debrief to validate their feelings about the lost effort, clearly explain the market context behind the pivot, and realign current tasks to the new roadmap.
Instruct the team to pause all work while you lobby executive leadership to let you finish the original project scope first.
Immediately send out new project assignments without acknowledging the discarded work, urging the team to move on quickly.

scenario: Company leadership mandates a transition from a remote-first work environment to a hybrid model requiring three mandatory days in the office. Your team expresses intense pushback and fear of disruption.

options.text: Host an open forum to listen to specific concerns, clarify the business rationale, and empower team leads to establish flexible, collaborative in-office schedules within the mandated guidelines.
Secretly tell your top performers that they can ignore the mandate and remain fully remote to prevent them from resigning.
Tell the team that corporate rules are non-negotiable and that anyone refusing to comply should look for opportunities elsewhere.
Draft a petition to executive leadership signed by your department demanding a complete reversal of the policy.

scenario: A structural re-organization merges two departments into your scope. The incoming team brings established workflows that conflict directly with your current team's processes.

options.text: Mandate that the incoming team immediately adopt your team's existing processes to establish uniformity and authority.
Form a joint process committee represented by members of both original teams to evaluate both workflows and build an optimized, unified operating model.
Allow both groups to continue operating under their separate legacy processes indefinitely to avoid immediate friction.
Adopt the incoming team's processes entirely to make them feel welcomed, regardless of current team efficiency.

scenario: Your organization institutes a corporate-wide hiring freeze during a period when your department's workload is projected to increase by 25% over the next two quarters.

options.text: Require your team to work mandatory overtime to ensure all prospective deliverables are met on time.
Audit current department projects, ruthlessly deprioritize non-essential activities with stakeholder buy-in, and streamline workflows to focus strictly on high-impact deliverables.
Submit repeated emergency requests to HR for hiring freeze exceptions without modifying current department commitments.
Maintain standard working hours and let deliverables slip past deadlines to demonstrate to executive leadership that the hiring freeze is unworkable.

scenario: A veteran team lead on your team, who is highly influential among peers, actively expresses skepticism and passive-aggressive resistance toward a newly introduced agile methodology.

options.text: Reassign the team lead to an individual contributor role immediately to remove their influence from team discussions.
Meet 1-on-1 with the lead to address their specific concerns, involve them directly as a co-designer in adapting the methodology to the team's needs, and leverage their influence to drive adoption.
Ignore their resistance publicly and hope that seeing others adopt the new methodology will eventually persuade them.
Reprimand the lead in front of the team during sprint planning to establish clear boundaries regarding change resistance.

scenario: An unexpected regulatory update requires your team to implement strict documentation compliance measures within two weeks, disrupting planned feature development.

options.text: Halt feature development immediately, clearly map out the compliance steps, assign clear roles, and re-baseline sprint goals to guarantee full regulatory alignment by the deadline.
Instruct the team to complete compliance documentation in their spare time while keeping feature development as the primary priority.
Ask the legal department for an extension, assuming regulatory deadlines usually have grace periods.
Assign the entire compliance workload to a single junior team member so the rest of the team remains focused on sprint goals.

scenario: Your organization is adopting Generative AI tools to automate core operational tasks. Several employees express anxiety that the technology will eventually render their roles redundant.

options.text: Tell employees that AI adoption is inevitable and that those who do not adapt quickly will naturally fall behind.
Address role security fears openly, emphasize how AI will elevate their roles from manual execution to strategic oversight, and launch upskilling initiatives to build AI competencies.
Minimize the impact of the tools by telling the team the company is just experimenting and that their day-to-day work won't really change.
Delay integrating AI tools into your department's workflow until corporate policy provides explicit job protection guarantees.

scenario: You take over a department that has gone through three restructuring efforts in two years. The team is suffering from change fatigue, cynicism, and low engagement.

options.text: Announce another major operational shakeup right away to establish your leadership authority and clear out lingering inertia.
Focus first on creating stability by securing quick operational wins, establishing transparent communication, and involving the team directly before introducing further changes.
Promise the team that no further operational or structural changes will occur while you are their manager.
Host a social event to boost team morale while keeping current performance expectations unchanged.

scenario: A key client changes their primary project requirements drastically late in the execution phase, threatening your team's planned delivery schedule.

options.text: Refuse the client's changes, citing the signed original project scope and terms.
Evaluate the technical and resource impact of the new requirements, present a revised timeline and budget to the client, and adjust internal sprint priorities accordingly.
Accept all requested changes immediately without adjusting the delivery schedule, forcing your team to work late hours.
Escalate the situation to senior leadership, asking them to handle the client negotiation while your team continues working on the original plan.

scenario: A budget cut forces your company to cancel an external vendor contract that previously handled a significant portion of your team's administrative tasks.

options.text: Distribute the vendor's administrative tasks evenly across current staff without reviewing or altering their existing core project responsibilities.
Conduct an operational review to eliminate redundant steps, automate repetitive elements of the administrative tasks, and adjust project timelines to absorb remaining essential work.
Absorb all the vendor's previous administrative workload yourself to protect your team from extra tasks.
Instruct your team to stop performing non-core administrative tasks entirely, regardless of operational impacts.

scenario: Your organization shifts from an annual performance review process to a continuous quarterly feedback model. A few of your frontline managers feel overwhelmed by the additional administrative cadence.

options.text: Tell the frontline managers that quarterly reviews are required HR policy and must be completed regardless of operational friction.
Provide frontline managers with streamlined feedback templates, run coaching sessions on effective short-form check-ins, and help them integrate feedback into existing 1-on-1 meetings.
Allow managers to complete continuous feedback informally without documenting updates in the system.
Conduct the quarterly reviews for the frontline managers' direct reports yourself to relieve their administrative workload.

scenario: A cross-functional partner team changes their data platform, requiring your team to adapt their data intake pipelines within three weeks to prevent reporting outages.

options.text: Complain to the partner team's director about the short notice and demand a three-month delay in platform migration.
Organize a technical alignment session with the partner team, create a temporary bridge solution to ensure data continuity, and schedule pipeline updates into upcoming sprints.
Instruct your team to build a completely independent data collection framework to avoid future partner dependencies.
Require your team to pause all current deliverables immediately to rewrite the data intake pipelines fully.

scenario: You are rolling out a new cross-departmental approval workflow that reduces bureaucratic steps, but several senior leaders insist on continuing legacy manual sign-offs.

options.text: Schedule 1-on-1s with the senior leaders to demonstrate how the automated workflow maintains audit controls, addresses their governance concerns, and speeds up project velocity.
Bypass the senior leaders entirely and process approvals using the new system without their involvement.
Modify the new system to re-insert the legacy manual approval steps for those specific senior leaders.
Report the non-compliant senior leaders to executive leadership for obstructing operational modernization.

scenario: Economic shifts force your company to pivot focus from high-growth customer acquisition to cost optimization and customer retention. Your team's targets must change immediately.

options.text: Re-align department KPIs toward retention metrics, hold a team workshop to translate the strategic shift into practical daily actions, and retrain staff on retention tools.
Maintain existing acquisition targets alongside new retention targets to ensure no operational ground is lost.
Inform the team of the target changes via email and expect them to adjust their metrics independently.
Focus exclusively on cost-cutting measures within the department while leaving core service delivery unchanged.

scenario: A major security vulnerability is discovered in an application your team relies on daily, requiring an immediate shutdown of the tool for an estimated five days.

options.text: Tell your team to take on light administrative duties and wait until the application is fully restored by IT.
Activate pre-planned manual workarounds, prioritize critical client-facing workflows, and communicate realistic timeline expectations clearly to internal stakeholders.
Authorize your team to use unapproved personal tools temporarily to keep daily productivity metrics high.
Escalate to IT leadership daily, demanding emergency access exceptions for key team members.

scenario: Your company merges with a former competitor. Your team is tasked with adopting the acquired company's technical infrastructure, which your team considers inferior.

options.text: Refuse to adopt the new infrastructure, presenting technical reports to executive leadership proving your original system is superior.
Acknowledge the team's technical concerns, focus discussions on strategic integration goals, and actively involve your engineers in identifying integration improvements.
Publicly agree with your team's criticisms of the new system while complying with integration deadlines on paper.
Outsource the system migration to an external contractor so your team doesn't have to deal with the inferior tool.

scenario: A shift in company strategy requires your team to start managing projects using a matrix reporting structure, where team members report to both you and a functional project lead.

options.text: Establish a joint alignment session with the functional leads to define clear boundaries, build a shared RACI framework, and streamline communication channels for team reports.
Instruct team members to prioritize your direct assignments over functional project lead tasks whenever conflicts arise.
Tell team members to navigate competing directives independently to build professional resilience.
Step back entirely from task-level directives and focus solely on administrative line management duties.

scenario: Your organization rolls out a new Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) hiring framework. One of your hiring managers believes the added evaluation steps slow down recruitment.

options.text: Allow the hiring manager to skip the new evaluation steps for urgent open requisitions.
Discuss the strategic importance of mitigating bias in talent acquisition, walk through the new framework, and partner with talent acquisition to streamline candidate screening.
Warn the hiring manager that failing to follow the framework will result in formal HR escalation.
Take over candidate screening for the hiring manager's open positions to ensure compliance without debate.

scenario: Your product team's core software offering is being transitioned to a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) subscription model, requiring your implementation team to shift from long customization cycles to rapid onboarding.

options.text: Hold training workshops to upskill staff on rapid onboarding methodology, adjust performance metrics to reflect onboarding speed, and establish feedback loops with product development.
Continue offering deep customizations for high-value clients while using rapid onboarding for smaller accounts.
Inform the team that their current skill set is outdated and encourage them to quickly adapt on their own.
Request additional headcount to manage the legacy custom accounts while hiring new staff for rapid onboarding.

scenario: A new regional regulatory standard mandates that all customer data processing must occur locally, invalidating your department's centralized cloud setup.

options.text: Form a task force with legal and IT architecture teams to map out a compliant regional data framework, prioritizing critical data pathways to prevent operational downtime.
Continue using the centralized cloud setup while legal applies for regulatory compliance waivers.
Pause regional operations until a fully compliant infrastructure can be designed and deployed.
Delegate the technical setup completely to regional team leads without establishing a unified compliance timeline.

scenario: Your team's physical office location is being consolidated into a smaller space with hot-desking practices, disrupting long-standing desk arrangements and personal working habits.

options.text: Tell the team to adapt quickly, as workspace changes are minor compared to business deliverables.
Acknowledge the disruption, establish clear, fair team norms for workspace sharing, and leverage flexible hybrid scheduling to optimize office attendance.
Assign permanent seats informally within your team's designated zone in violation of the hot-desking policy.
Allow employees to work entirely from home until the initial friction of space consolidation settles.

scenario: Senior leadership initiates a shift toward OKR (Objectives and Key Results) goal-setting. Your team is struggling to transition from activity-based goals to outcome-based metrics.

options.text: Write the team's OKRs yourself and assign them to individuals to ensure proper formatting.
Conduct collaborative goal-setting sessions, coach the team on defining measurable key results, and iteratively refine their draft OKRs with real-world project examples.
Let the team continue using activity-based goals while converting them into OKR terminology for executive reporting.
Direct team members to complete online training modules on OKRs and resubmit their goals independently.

scenario: An key enterprise system upgrade fails during weekend deployment, forcing your department to operate on manual recovery processes on Monday morning.

options.text: Cancel all client meetings and order the team to focus strictly on system restoration alongside IT.
Brief the team at the start of the day, deploy defined business continuity procedures, assign task owners for manual processing, and maintain transparent client communications.
Send staff home for the day to avoid lost productivity and confusion while IT resolves the issue.
Have team members process work as best they can without establishing centralized tracking for manual entries.

scenario: Your organization shifts its go-to-market strategy from mid-market clients to enterprise accounts, requiring longer sales cycles and more complex technical delivery.

options.text: Expect staff to adapt to enterprise complexity immediately using their existing execution templates.
Assess current capability gaps, implement training on enterprise account management, and pair junior staff with experienced enterprise lead staff.
Focus department efforts exclusively on legacy mid-market clients to protect near-term revenue metrics.
Request that senior executive leadership handle all enterprise account interactions until your team is restructured.

scenario: A company-wide initiative mandates that all departments publish open APIs and internal documentation to enable self-service across teams, adding work to your backlog.

options.text: Treat the documentation mandate as a low priority, completing it only when primary team deliverables are finished.
Integrate documentation tasks into current sprint definitions of done, highlight long-term efficiency gains to the team, and allocate dedicated capacity for API exposure.
Assign a temporary intern to write the documentation to prevent interrupting core staff deliverables.
Request a budget exception to hire an external technical writer to handle the documentation burden.

scenario: Your company introduces a formal job architecture framework that reclassifies several job titles and salary bands within your team, creating anxiety regarding career progression.

options.text: Advise team members to take title concerns directly to HR since compensation frameworks are outside manager control.
Schedule 1-on-1s to explain the career framework transparently, map individual roles to clear competency levels, and build tailored growth plans for advancement.
Assure disappointed employees that you will bypass the new framework to get them promotions under the old criteria.
Address the title changes in a group meeting and encourage the team to focus on daily work rather than job titles.

scenario: A shift in company procurement policies forces your team to switch from a familiar, highly responsive software vendor to an enterprise-approved vendor with slower support.

options.text: Establish operational SLAs with the new vendor, adjust internal project risk buffers to account for support times, and train team leads on escalation paths.
Continue using the original software vendor on corporate credit cards under petty expense thresholds.
Complain to procurement daily whenever vendor responses are delayed to force a policy rollback.
Encourage the team to rely on informal community forums for technical troubleshooting instead of the new vendor.

scenario: An internal audit reveals that your department's reporting methods do not align with company standards, requiring a complete redesign of your weekly status dashboards.

options.text: Collaborate with the audit team to understand the standard requirements, engage staff to redesign the reporting tools, and automate data collection to minimize overhead.
Manually reformat team reports yourself every week to shield staff from the administrative change.
Argue against the audit findings, maintaining that your team's custom reporting method is more useful.
Delegate dashboard creation to individual team members without providing standardized templates or guidance.

scenario: Your organization introduces a new cross-functional rotational program, requiring you to host temporary team members for six-month cycles while sending core staff elsewhere.

options.text: Assign rotational staff basic administrative tasks to ensure core project velocity is maintained by remaining permanent staff.
Design structured onboarding playbooks for rotational incoming staff, assign buddy mentors, and integrate them into core deliverables to maximize knowledge transfer.
Opt out of the rotational program citing high technical specialization requirements in your team.
Treat rotational staff as observers and avoid giving them primary project ownership during their tenure.

scenario: Executive leadership accelerates a product delivery schedule by one month to capitalize on a competitor's vulnerability, creating high pressure for your team.

options.text: Mandate weekend work for the team to meet the accelerated deadline without altering the project scope.
Review project scope to identify core essentials for an accelerated MVP, deprioritize non-critical features, and secure temporary cross-team support to hit the new date.
Inform executive leadership that accelerating the schedule is impossible without causing widespread resignation.
Maintain current feature scope and encourage staff to work faster during regular working hours.

scenario: Your department is transitioning from dedicated project teams to a flexible resource pool model where team members are assigned based on real-time project demand.

options.text: Resist the resource pool model and attempt to keep your core project team intact informally.
Implement centralized skill-tracking tools, establish clear assignment criteria, and conduct regular check-ins to ensure staff feel supported across changing project assignments.
Allow team members to choose their own project assignments from the pool on a first-come, first-served basis.
Assign pool resources strictly based on staff availability without considering skill matching or development goals.

scenario: Your organization shifts to a fully asynchronous communication model across global offices, reducing synchronous status meetings drastically.

options.text: Establish clear documentation protocols, train staff on effective written updates, and set explicit response-time expectations for asynchronous channels.
Continue scheduling regular status meetings for your immediate local team while using asynchronous communication for global peers.
Eliminate all status updates entirely and rely on ad-hoc messaging whenever questions arise.
Require team members to submit detailed written daily activity logs to replace standup meetings.

scenario: A direct report who is otherwise technically solid routinely presents complex project updates laden with jargon and technical minutiae, causing executive stakeholders during quarterly reviews to tune out and miss key business risks.

options.text: Coach the report privately on executive communication frameworks (e.g., leading with bottom-line business impacts before technical details) and offer to review their presentation decks prior to executive meetings.
Take over presenting the executive updates yourself to ensure the leadership team receives clear, business-focused information.
Interrupt the report during the next executive meeting to translate their technical points into business terms on the spot.
Send the report an article on effective public speaking and tell them to simplify their slides for the next review.

scenario: During a cross-functional project kickoff, a peer manager from another department repeatedly cuts off your team members while they are speaking, dismissing their input as secondary to their own team's priorities.

options.text: Intervene calmly during the meeting to re-engage your team member by saying, 'I'd like to let [Name] finish their point first,' and discuss collaborative meeting norms privately with the peer afterward.
Call out the peer manager aggressively in the meeting to ensure your team feels defended and supported.
Say nothing during the meeting to avoid open confrontation, but tell your team members afterward not to take it personally.
Escalate the peer's unprofessional behavior directly to their department head immediately after the meeting ends.

scenario: You need to inform your department that due to budget realignments, a multi-quarter software initiative they spent months planning has been canceled, and their focus must shift to maintaining legacy systems.

options.text: Send a formal company memo stating the project cancellation details and instructing everyone to update their task boards immediately.
Hold an all-hands meeting to transparently share the strategic business context behind the decision, validate their hard work, and hold an open Q&A session to address concerns.
Delay sharing the news for a few weeks while you try to find alternative funding to avoid demoralizing the team.
Break the news to team leads first in private 1-on-1s and ask them to cascade the message informally to their respective sub-teams.

scenario: A frontline manager reporting to you avoids giving critical performance feedback to a struggling direct report because they fear damaging their friendly rapport, resulting in ongoing project errors.

options.text: Step in and deliver the critical performance feedback to the struggling employee yourself to ensure it is communicated accurately.
Role-play the feedback conversation with the frontline manager, help them structure SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) feedback, and follow up afterward to discuss how it went.
Issue a formal written reprimand to the frontline manager for failing to execute their management duties.
Sit in on the 1-on-1 conversation between the frontline manager and employee to jump in if the manager hesitates.

scenario: You receive conflicting communication from two executive leaders regarding the core priority for your department this quarter, leaving your team confused about resource allocation.

options.text: Pick the priority advocated by the higher-ranking executive and instruct your team to execute against that vision.
Schedule a brief alignment meeting with both executive leaders together, presenting the resource trade-offs and seeking a unified directive for your department.
Instruct your team to work on both priorities simultaneously by splitting their working hours 50/50.
Ask your direct reports to choose which priority aligns best with their day-to-day expertise and execute accordingly.

scenario: A key stakeholder sends an angry, highly accusatory email to you and your director, claiming your team intentionally hid project delays during the last status update.

options.text: Reply-all immediately with a detailed, defensive point-by-point rebuttal proving that the stakeholder's claims are incorrect.
Acknowledge the stakeholder's email calmly, request a quick phone or video call to address their concerns, and follow up with a clear action plan documenting project status.
Ignore the email and ask your director to deal with the stakeholder directly.
Send a private email to the stakeholder providing the facts, while keeping the executive director off the reply chain to de-escalate quietly.

scenario: Your department relies heavily on asynchronous communication (Slack/Teams), but vital project decisions are routinely lost in long, unstructured chat threads, leading to missed dependencies.

options.text: Mandate that all project decisions must now take place in live daily video meetings instead of chat channels.
Establish clear communication protocols (e.g., using dedicated decision threads, updating project hubs, tagging owners) and model these behaviors consistently.
Delete inactive chat channels and tell team members they will be reprimanded if key decisions are made in chat.
Appoint a junior team member to manually read all chat threads and compile a weekly decision log.

scenario: During an all-hands meeting, an employee asks a challenging question about recent executive compensation increases during a company-wide cost-cutting period. The room goes silent.

options.text: Dismiss the question as inappropriate for an all-hands forum and immediately move on to the next topic.
Acknowledge the difficulty and sensitivity of the question, address the business context transparently within the bounds of what can be shared, and offer to follow up on unresolved points.
Pretend you did not hear the question clearly and ask for a different question from the audience.
State that executive compensation is strictly determined by the Board of Directors and suggest scheduling a separate HR session later.

scenario: A high-performing senior individual contributor consistently provides feedback to junior peers in a harsh, blunt manner that leaves them feeling demoralized and reluctant to ask for help.

options.text: Praise the senior contributor's high technical accuracy while gently asking them to try to be nicer to junior staff.
Meet 1-on-1 with the senior contributor to highlight specific instances of harsh delivery, explain the impact on team psychological safety, and coach them on constructive delivery techniques.
Reassign all junior staff away from the senior contributor so they no longer need to interact.
Publicly correct the senior contributor the next time they use a blunt tone during a code or document review.

scenario: You are rolling out a new software integration process across three global offices in different time zones. Communication about process changes has felt disjointed and uneven.

options.text: Schedule a mandatory live briefing at a time convenient for your local office and record it for global teams to watch later.
Develop a centralized, asynchronous communication kit (written documentation, short video walkthroughs, and localized regional Q&A leads) to ensure consistent information delivery.
Require all global team leads to stay up late or wake up early to attend a single mandatory alignment call.
Send a long email detailing the operational changes and ask regional leads to explain it to their local teams as they see fit.

scenario: You notice that during team retrospectives, team members only share superficial praise and avoid discussing process bottlenecks or failures, fearing conflict.

options.text: Cancel retrospectives since the team clearly feels everything is going well and the meetings are unproductive.

Introduce anonymous input tools prior to retrospectives, openly share your own recent management missteps to model vulnerability, and frame process issues as system problems rather than personal failures.
Call out specific individuals during the retrospective and demand they share one thing that went wrong in their project.
Require every team member to submit at least two complaints in writing before attending the meeting.

scenario: A manager reporting to you presents quarterly metrics that look overly optimistic, intentionally omitting key data regarding customer churn that you know exists.

options.text: Fix the presentation slides yourself before sending them to executive leadership without discussing it with the manager.
Address the omission privately with the manager, reinforce the necessity of transparent reporting for executive decision-making, and require them to update the report with accurate churn data.
Reprimand the manager publicly during the metrics review session to emphasize company Integrity standards.
Allow the presentation to proceed as is, but verbally mention the churn data during the executive meeting.

scenario: A newly promoted team lead struggles to summarize monthly department accomplishments for upper management, submitting multi-page essays that leadership refuses to read.

options.text: Write the monthly summary yourself and tell the team lead to watch how you do it moving forward.
Provide the lead with a structured executive summary template (e.g., Key Wins, Risks, Milestones), establish word-count constraints, and review initial drafts together.
Reject the submission and tell the lead to make it shorter without providing further guidelines.
Ask a peer team lead who excels at executive reporting to handle summaries for both teams.

scenario: You conduct an anonymous survey regarding communication effectiveness in your division. Results show staff feel executive leadership is out of touch with day-to-day operational realities.

options.text: Keep the survey results private from executive leadership to protect your team from executive backlash.

Synthesize the survey themes, present the findings constructively to executive leadership alongside actionable recommendations (e.g., operational 'skip-level' syncs), and communicate the action plan back to staff.
Send the raw survey data directly to executive leadership and let them decide how to respond.
Host a department town hall to explain why executive leadership makes the decisions they do, defending their current approach.

scenario: A member of your team who recently received constructive feedback regarding document accuracy has become silent in 1-on-1s and responds with brief one-word answers.

options.text: Ignore the emotional shift and focus strictly on task updates during 1-on-1s, assuming they will get over it.
Gently bring up the change in interaction style, invite them to share how they received the feedback, clarify your intent to support their growth, and check for mutual understanding.
Warn them that having a bad attitude regarding feedback will reflect negatively on their upcoming review.
Cancel upcoming 1-on-1s temporarily to give them space to process the feedback independently.

scenario: You need to negotiate a shared deadline extension with a peer manager whose team handles downstream testing for your product releases, but their team is already overworked.

options.text: Escalate the deadline issue directly to your shared director to mandate an extension for the peer's team.
Schedule a sync with the peer manager, explain the rationale for the extension, listen to their team's capacity constraints, and co-design a phased testing schedule that limits overtime.
Unilaterally shift your team's delivery date and notify the peer via email that testing deadlines must shift accordingly.
Offer to trade team resources or take on administrative tasks for their team in exchange for the testing extension.

scenario: A vendor key account manager repeatedly promises software capability updates during phone calls that are never reflected in the official contract or delivered on time.

options.text: Stop using the vendor software immediately and inform executive leadership of vendor breach of trust.
Summarize all verbal discussions in follow-up written emails, demand formal contractual amendments for future commitments, and schedule a monthly delivery review against documented milestones.
Accept the verbal promises and continue waiting, as building software features often takes longer than planned.
Refuse to pay current vendor invoices until the promised features are delivered.

scenario: You are hosting a skip-level 1-on-1 with a frontline individual contributor. They begin complaining extensively about their direct manager's micro-management style.

options.text: Agree with the contributor and promise to reprimand their direct manager immediately.

Listen empathetically without validating unverified claims, ask clarifying questions, encourage the contributor to give direct feedback to their manager, and offer coaching on how to have that conversation.
Cut the contributor off and state that discussing manager performance with skip-levels violates company hierarchy.
Take notes and tell the contributor you will investigate the situation quietly with HR.

scenario: A project update call with external clients turns tense when an engineer on your team blurted out that a critical feature is broken and might take weeks to fix, causing client panic.

options.text: Publicly scold the engineer during the call to show the client you hold your team accountable.
Step in calmly on the call to contextualize the technical issue, outline the immediate risk mitigation steps, promise a documented update by end-of-day, and debrief privately with the engineer later.
End the client call abruptly, citing technical difficulties, to figure out what to say.
Contradict the engineer immediately on the call, telling the client the engineer is mistaken and everything is fine.

scenario: An employee approaches you expressing that they do not feel comfortable providing upward feedback to you during formal performance cycles because you are their rating manager.

options.text: Tell them that providing upward feedback is a required part of the review process and they need to participate.
Validate their perspective, explain how upward feedback helps you improve as a leader, suggest third-party or HR-facilitated feedback channels if preferred, and model openness to critique.
Exempt them from filling out the upward feedback form permanently.
Ask them to submit their feedback to a peer on the team who can relay it to you anonymously.

scenario: A sudden organizational crisis requires your department to change daily operating procedures immediately. Information is changing hour-by-hour.

options.text: Wait until all details are 100% finalized before sending a single comprehensive update to avoid confusing the team.
Establish a predictable daily briefing cadence (e.g., 9 AM updates), clearly separate known facts from unknown variables, and provide immediate channels for emergent questions.
Send real-time chat alerts every time a minor detail changes throughout the day to keep everyone informed.
Delegate all crisis communication to team leads while you focus on attending executive crisis briefings.

scenario: A remote employee consistently turns off their video camera during small interactive team syncs, and team members complain that they feel disconnected from them during discussions.

options.text: Institute a strict mandatory 'cameras-on' policy for all team meetings across the department.

Have a private 1-on-1 to ask about their experience in meetings, explore whether there are technical or personal constraints, communicate the team's desire for connection, and find a comfortable middle ground.
Call out the employee during the next meeting, asking them to turn their camera on so everyone can see them.
Ignore the issue as long as the employee completes their assigned tasks on time.

scenario: You notice that an important policy update regarding expense approvals was completely missed by half your department, despite you sending a company email about it two weeks ago.

options.text: Resend the original email with 'SECOND NOTICE' in the subject line and threaten to reject non-compliant expenses.
Recognize single-channel email fatigue; highlight the key policy changes in team meetings, pin a summary in main chat channels, and update manager 1-on-1 check-in templates.
Refuse to process expenses for anyone who failed to read the email correctly.
Require all employees to reply 'I agree' to the policy email before processing future expense claims.

scenario: A talented engineer on your team gets visibly defensive and argumentative whenever code review comments are left on their pull requests, leading peers to avoid giving them feedback.

options.text: Instruct peers to stop leaving review comments and instead bring all code feedback directly to you to deliver.

Discuss the pattern privately with the engineer, clarify that code reviews focus on product quality rather than personal skill, establish objective review criteria, and coach them on receptive feedback behaviors.
Reassign the engineer to work strictly on solo projects where code reviews are unnecessary.
Require all code review comments for this engineer to be submitted anonymously.

scenario: You are leading a project presentation to potential internal client departments. One of your department leads keeps answering questions meant for another team member.

options.text: Interrupt the lead forcefully during the call and command them to let others speak.

Facilitate the meeting actively by directing incoming questions specifically to designated owners (e.g., '[Name], would you address the analytics part?'), and debrief privately with the lead afterward.
Let the lead answer all questions to present a unified, confident front to the internal client.
Text the lead during the presentation telling them to stop talking.

scenario: You realize that a performance framework document you shared with your team contained vague, ambiguous criteria that created widespread confusion regarding promotion expectations.

options.text: Wait until annual review time to clarify the criteria individually during performance rating discussions.
Own the ambiguity transparently, publish an updated version with concrete, objective criteria and real-world examples, and host a Q&A session to walk through the changes.
Insist that the framework is clear and tell employees they are overthinking the requirements.
Quietly update the document online without making an announcement and hope people notice the improvements.

scenario: A cross-functional committee member leaves meetings promising to deliver key assets, but consistently fails to follow through, stating later that they didn't realize it was an official commitment.

options.text: Complain about the member's unreliability during the next open steering committee meeting.
Implement formal written meeting summaries documenting action items, explicit owners, and agreed deadlines immediately after meetings, requiring explicit confirmation from attendees.
Remove the member from the committee without consulting their line manager.
Take over delivering the assets yourself to ensure project deadlines do not slip.

scenario: An individual contributor on your team approaches you to pitch a new workflow tool, but their pitch is unstructured, disorganized, and lacks data on cost or implementation.

options.text: Reject the proposal immediately, telling them not to waste time on unvetted software tools.
Applaud their initiative, explain what key information leadership requires for tool evaluation (ROI, security, implementation effort), and offer a framework to help them refine the pitch.
Approve the tool purchase immediately to encourage team innovation and morale.
Take their rough idea and research the costs and implementation details yourself to present to leadership.

scenario: A manager reporting to you delivers positive feedback during an employee's annual review, but assigns them a 'Below Expectations' rating, creating shock and anger.

options.text: Override the manager's rating to 'Meets Expectations' so it aligns with the verbal feedback delivered.

Pause the review cycle, coach the manager on eliminating feedback disconnects (ensuring performance issues are communicated immediately rather than delayed), and guide them on conducting a transparent alignment meeting.
Tell the employee that annual ratings are final and that they should have realized their work was subpar.
Attend the follow-up performance conversation yourself to explain the low rating on behalf of the manager.

scenario: You need to deliver feedback to a high-value customer about their internal team's toxic communication style toward your implementation staff, risking contract renewal.

options.text: Tell your implementation staff to tolerate the communication style because the account revenue is too valuable to lose.

Schedule an executive alignment call with the customer lead, focus on objective behavior logs, frame professional working standards as essential for project success, and establish clear communication protocols.
Send a harsh warning email to the customer stating that services will be terminated immediately if tone doesn't change.
Replace your current implementation staff with more resilient personnel who won't complain about customer behavior.

scenario: Two sub-teams within your department are using conflicting terminology for the same operational processes, leading to errors in cross-team data handoffs.

options.text: Mandate that Sub-Team A drop their terminology and adopt Sub-Team B's naming conventions completely.
Bring key leads from both sub-teams together to establish a standardized domain glossary, document it in central knowledge hubs, and update workflow templates.
Allow both teams to use their preferred terminology and build automated translation scripts to map data handoffs.
Reprimand both team leads for failing to align their communication standards earlier.

scenario: During an important strategic presentation to potential partners, your manager misstates key performance data regarding your department's capacity.

options.text: Interrupt your manager immediately during the presentation to correct the data in front of the partners.
Wait for a natural transition or Q&A segment to clarify the numbers gently, or brief your manager privately right after the call so a corrected summary can be sent.
Say nothing at all and adjust your department's working capacity to match the incorrect data presented.
Send a private chat message to the external partners during the meeting with the correct data.

scenario: Your team's workload is scheduled to double next sprint due to regulatory reporting requirements. The team is already working at near-full capacity.

options.text: Tell the team to work harder for the next few weeks and promise that things will quiet down eventually.
Communicate the upcoming mandate transparently, review current backlog tasks together to deprioritize non-essential work, and secure temporary cross-team support or overtime compensation.
Keep the upcoming workload increase a secret until the sprint begins to prevent early panic.
Refuse to take on the regulatory reporting requirements, stating that your team is at capacity.

scenario: Your department has been focused exclusively on short-term tactical bug fixes and maintenance requests for three consecutive quarters, leaving no bandwidth for developing new strategic platform capabilities aligned with company goals.

options.text: Analyze recurring support trends to automate tactical maintenance, and propose allocating a dedicated 30% capacity block in upcoming roadmaps for long-term strategic capabilities.
Instruct your team to reject all future maintenance requests from partner departments so they can focus 100% on strategic projects.
Continue prioritizing maintenance requests as they arrive to satisfy immediate internal stakeholder needs and protect quarterly SLAs.
Ask your team to work additional hours on weekends to build strategic features while maintaining current maintenance output.

scenario: Executive leadership communicates a broad 3-year vision to become an AI-driven organization, but your direct reports are confused about what this high-level vision actually means for their daily technical deliverables.

options.text: Facilitate a department workshop to break down the 3-year AI vision into concrete annual OKRs, clear workflow applications, and specific skill development milestones for the team.
Forward the executive vision deck to your team via email and instruct them to figure out how to integrate AI tools into their current projects.
Tell your team to ignore the vision deck for now and focus strictly on their immediate sprint commitments until explicit mandates are issued.
Rewrite all current team job descriptions to include 'AI expertise' without changing daily task expectations or providing training.

scenario: An established product line in your portfolio generates steady baseline revenue but shows declining growth metrics, while an emerging product line offers high growth potential but carries significant operational risk.

options.text: Reallocate all department budget and personnel away from the established product line to bet entirely on the emerging product.
Conduct a portfolio analysis to streamline operational costs on the mature product, freeing up strategic capital and talent to nurture the high-growth emerging product sustainably.
Focus all department efforts on the mature product line to protect guaranteed revenue, ignoring the emerging market trend.
Maintain equal resource distribution across both product lines regardless of growth rates or market potential.

scenario: You notice that a cross-functional partner team is building an internal data pipeline that duplicates an initiative your own department completed two quarters ago.

options.text: Schedule an alignment session with the partner team lead to share your existing architecture, offer reusable components, and co-design a unified cross-departmental roadmap.
Allow the partner team to finish their build so they can learn from their own operational experience.
Report the partner team to executive management for wasting company resources on duplicate work.
Send a copy of your team's code repository to the partner team lead with a brief email suggesting they use it.

scenario: Industry market data indicates that a core technical skill set heavily utilized by your team will become obsolete within two to three years due to automation.

options.text: Keep current operations unchanged until the technology actually becomes obsolete, then hire new staff with updated skills.
Design a strategic upskilling program, allocating time and training budgets now to transition your current workforce toward emerging core competencies.
Inform team members that their skill set is dying and advise them to seek training outside of work hours.
Immediately stop using the legacy technology and mandate adoption of modern tools before training plans are in place.

scenario: During annual planning, your department is offered a choice: execute a safe, incremental project guaranteed to hit targets, or pursue a transformative strategic project with higher business impact but a 30% risk of failure.

options.text: Choose the incremental project to guarantee 100% target achievement and protect team performance bonuses.
Pitch the transformative project to leadership alongside a comprehensive risk-mitigation plan, phased milestones, and clear criteria for early course-correction.
Commit to executing both projects simultaneously without requesting extra budget or resources.
Select the transformative project but scale down its strategic scope until the risk profile matches the incremental project.

scenario: A major client offers a lucrative short-term contract, but fulfilling it requires your team to build custom features that deviate significantly from your long-term core product architecture.

options.text: Accept the contract immediately to boost current quarter revenue, promising your team you will clean up technical debt later.
Evaluate the strategic alignment, negotiate a solution with the client that solves their core need using standard architecture, or decline if it creates unsustainable technical drag.
Reject the client request flatly without exploring alternative solutions or evaluating revenue impact.
Outsource the custom build to an external contractor to protect internal bandwidth, despite long-term maintenance costs.

scenario: Your organization's primary competitor launches a aggressive pricing model that is attracting mid-market customers away from your core business offerings.

options.text: Demand that executive leadership slash your product's pricing immediately to match the competitor's rates.
Conduct a strategic analysis of customer value drivers, identify your unique product differentiators, and propose repositioning or enhancing value-add services rather than engaging in a price war.
Ignore the competitor's strategy, assuming existing customers will remain loyal regardless of price differences.
Direct your sales and marketing teams to discount products on an ad-hoc basis for complaining clients.

scenario: You notice that individual teams within your department are optimizing for their local operational metrics (e.g., ticket resolution speed) at the expense of overall customer satisfaction metrics.

options.text: Eliminate local operational metrics entirely and evaluate individual team performance solely on customer satisfaction.
Realign department incentive structures by connecting local operational metrics directly to end-to-end customer journey outcomes, educating team leads on systemic dependencies.
Issue a stern warning to team leads demanding they stop ignoring customer satisfaction.
Add customer satisfaction checks as a manual approval step controlled exclusively by you before tickets can be closed.

scenario: Your company is planning an expansion into international markets, which will require significant localization and regulatory changes for your team's core applications over the next 12 months.

options.text: Wait until international sales contracts are signed before assessing architecture or technical requirements.
Proactively initiate an architectural discovery phase now, building a modular roadmap that incorporates international compliance requirements into current sprint cycles.
Halt all current feature development to rewrite your entire system for internationalization immediately.
Request that executive leadership hire a separate international engineering team to handle localization.
