scenario: Your team's current primary revenue-generating channel is experiencing organic traffic decay, but team leads resist investing time into exploring new unproven distribution channels.

options.text: Force the team leads to abandon the legacy channel completely and focus 100% on new channels.
Present channel decay trends transparently, allocate a dedicated 'growth experiment' budget, and establish low-risk pilot criteria to explore emerging distribution avenues.
Increase marketing spend on the declining legacy channel to compensate for traffic decay.
Hire an external agency to manage the legacy channel while internal staff explores new channels.

scenario: Executive leadership requests a 3-year strategic roadmap for your department, but current market conditions are highly volatile and unpredictable.

options.text: Refuse to build a 3-year plan, stating that market volatility makes long-term planning useless.
Develop a vision-driven 3-year strategic framework focused on core capability pillars, combined with flexible, scenario-based 6-month tactical execution cycles.
Deliver a rigid, highly detailed 3-year execution plan with fixed dates, assuming market conditions won't change.
Copy the strategic roadmap of a successful competitor and present it as your department's plan.

scenario: A new corporate sustainability and governance mandate requires all departments to reduce infrastructure energy consumption and vendor waste by 20% over the next year.

options.text: Treat the mandate as a low-priority HR request and wait for compliance audits before making changes.
Lead a strategic review of cloud resource utilization and vendor efficiency, embedding sustainable resource management metrics directly into operational guidelines.
Arbitrarily shut down 20% of department servers and tools immediately to hit the metric target.
Delegate compliance completely to a junior employee without adjusting department operational standards.

scenario: Your department delivers high-quality internal tools, but other business units frequently complain that they were never informed about these tools or how to leverage them.

options.text: Tell complaining business units that it is their responsibility to check your department's internal portal for tool updates.
Establish a strategic internal product management function, implementing stakeholder communication plans, user onboarding sessions, and adoption tracking metrics.
Stop building new tools and focus strictly on supporting existing ones to prevent further communication gaps.
Send a monthly mass email detailing technical release notes to the entire company.

scenario: A core software partner announces a strategic shift that will end support for a key platform dependency your department relies on in 18 months.

options.text: Ignore the announcement for now and handle the migration when the support officially ends in 18 months.
Evaluate alternative replacement platforms, build a multi-phase migration roadmap, and begin incorporating foundational architecture changes into current sprint backlogs.
Lobby the software partner aggressively to continue supporting the legacy platform indefinitely.
Freeze all current feature development to complete a full platform migration within the next two months.

scenario: Your organization is shifting from a B2B model to a direct-to-consumer (B2C) model, requiring a complete shift in user experience, scalability, and operational support.

options.text: Apply legacy B2B workflows and systems to B2C users, assuming user expectations are essentially the same.
Conduct a strategic gap analysis comparing B2B vs B2C requirements, realign team competencies, and build a phased technology and operational transformation roadmap.
Request that executive leadership hire an entirely new department to handle B2C operations.
Launch a basic B2C interface using existing B2B backend architecture without assessing performance limits.

scenario: You observe that your department's strategic goals are frequently derailed by emergency requests from senior sales executives seeking to close individual deals.

options.text: Accept all emergency sales requests immediately to ensure revenue targets are hit, regardless of strategic roadmap impact.
Establish a formal intake and governance framework with sales leadership to evaluate emergency requests against strategic value, business impact, and capacity trade-offs.
Refuse to speak with sales executives and block all incoming non-roadmap requests entirely.
Allocate a fixed 50% of department capacity permanently to ad-hoc sales requests without evaluation criteria.

scenario: Your team has successfully automated a core process, reducing required operational effort by 40%. The team is unsure how to utilize the newly freed-up bandwidth.

options.text: Reduce team headcount by 40% to capture immediate operational cost savings for the organization.
Strategically reallocate the newly available capacity toward accelerating high-impact innovation initiatives and strategic technical debt reduction.
Allow team members to relax their working hours and maintain lower output expectations.
Assign the team additional low-value administrative tasks from other departments to keep them busy.

scenario: Your company is considering acquiring a smaller competitor. You are asked to participate in due diligence to evaluate their technical infrastructure and team capabilities.

options.text: Focus solely on listing bug counts and technical flaws to justify lowering the acquisition purchase price.
Conduct a holistic evaluation analyzing strategic cultural fit, architecture scalability, integration friction, and long-term synergy value for the combined organization.
Recommend rejecting the acquisition outright because integrating unfamiliar technical systems is always difficult.
Delegate the due diligence review to a frontline lead without providing evaluation frameworks.

scenario: Your department relies heavily on legacy proprietary software tools that carry high licensing costs and lack modern integration capabilities.

options.text: Continue paying for legacy licenses indefinitely to avoid the operational risk of tool migration.
Develop a multi-year open-source or modern SaaS transition strategy, highlighting license cost savings, enhanced agility, and risk mitigation to executive leadership.
Cancel all legacy licenses immediately to save money, forcing staff to use unsupported free tools.
Negotiate minor discounts with the legacy vendor without exploring modern platform alternatives.

scenario: During a period of rapid company growth, your team's operational processes are scaling poorly, resulting in increased error rates and communication bottlenecks.

options.text: Tell staff to pay closer attention to detail and work faster during peak execution hours.
Step back to analyze systemic bottlenecks, re-architect operational workflows for scale, and introduce automation and clear delegation boundaries.
Hire more staff to execute the existing inefficient process manually.
Scale down department output targets to match the throughput of the legacy process.

scenario: A shift in consumer privacy laws requires a fundamental redesign of how your department collects, stores, and processes user data across all applications.

options.text: Implement quick band-aid patches to pass immediate audits while leaving core data architecture intact.
Leverage the regulatory shift to strategically modernize data governance, adopting privacy-by-design architecture that enhances trust and operational efficiency.
Shut down data collection features entirely to avoid any legal compliance exposure.
Outsource compliance liability to a third-party data processor without modifying internal data flows.

scenario: You notice that your department's annual strategy is misaligned with the updated goals of the core revenue-generating sales and operations units.

options.text: Maintain your existing department strategy since it was already approved at the start of the year.
Initiate cross-departmental strategy alignment syncs to adjust your operational roadmap, ensuring your deliverables directly enable sales and operational success.
Complain to leadership that other business units are changing their goals without consulting you.
Completely abandon your department's technical goals to adopt sales targets directly.

scenario: Your department is tasked with driving digital transformation across traditional, offline operational units that are highly resistant to digital change.

options.text: Mandate the immediate shutdown of offline workflows to force digital platform usage.
Identify high-value operational pain points, build intuitive digital pilot tools, partner with influential frontline champions, and demonstrate clear productivity gains.
Build digital tools in isolation and hand them off without providing training or transformation support.
Report the traditional units' resistance to executive sponsors, asking them to enforce usage.

scenario: Your team is developing a strategic new product, but customer discovery feedback shows that a secondary feature is receiving far more enthusiasm than the main product core.

options.text: Ignore the customer feedback and continue building the main product core as originally envisioned.
Analyze the customer engagement data, present a strategic pivot proposal to executive sponsors, and focus development on making the enthusiastic feature the main value proposition.
Cancel the project entirely because the original strategic hypothesis was proven incorrect.
Finish building the main product core, then add the secondary feature as an optional add-on later.

scenario: Executive leadership introduces a company-wide initiative to reduce operational silos by encouraging cross-departmental talent sharing and joint OKRs.

options.text: Protect your best team members from participating in cross-departmental initiatives to keep department productivity high.
Proactively partner with peer managers to identify shared strategic priorities, map joint OKRs, and create talent exchange opportunities that build organizational capability.
Assign low-performing team members to cross-departmental initiatives to satisfy the mandate.
Wait for executive leadership to explicitly assign specific joint OKRs to your department.

scenario: Your company is preparing for a public IPO or major funding round within the next 18 months, requiring heightened rigor in financial modeling, compliance, and governance.

options.text: Continue daily operations unchanged until formal IPO audit teams arrive.
Audit department governance, establish rigorous reporting metrics, streamline technical documentation, and align operational spending with investor due diligence standards.
Freeze all product development initiatives to focus 100% on financial governance documentation.
Outsource governance audits to external legal firms without involving internal department leads.

scenario: A key strategic vendor changes their pricing model, resulting in a projected 50% increase in software operating costs for your department next year.

options.text: Absorb the cost increase without review and request a budget addition from finance.
Conduct a usage audit to trim unnecessary licenses, evaluate competitive vendor alternatives, and leverage procurement negotiation to mitigate strategic financial impact.
Cancel the vendor contract immediately without identifying an alternative software solution.
Instruct team members to share user credentials to bypass license count restrictions.

scenario: Your organization's core customer base is aging, and market research indicates younger demographics prefer mobile-first, self-service digital experiences.

options.text: Continue focusing exclusively on the aging core customer base to protect current cash flows.
Formulate a strategic digital product roadmap that modernizes self-service capabilities for younger demographics while maintaining core service stability for existing users.
Deprecate legacy support tools immediately to force older customers to switch to mobile channels.
Launch a separate unbranded mobile application without integrating it into core operational systems.

scenario: You notice that your department excels at generating new ideas and strategic roadmaps, but consistently struggles with operational execution and finishing deliverables.

options.text: Stop setting strategic goals and focus exclusively on short-term daily task management.
Implement structured execution governance (e.g., clear RACI frameworks, milestone tracking, accountability check-ins) to bridge the gap between strategic vision and delivery.
Blame team members for lack of discipline and increase daily micromanagement.
Hire external project managers to take over execution entirely while staff focuses on strategy.

scenario: A sudden shift in trade policies or tariffs increases the unit cost of key hardware components essential for your department's physical product releases.

options.text: Pass the cost increase directly to customers without analyzing market demand price elasticity.
Partner with supply chain and engineering teams to explore alternative component designs, re-evaluate vendor sourcing, and optimize production processes to offset margin erosion.
Halt product manufacturing completely until tariffs are removed.
Compromise product build quality by using unverified cheap components.

scenario: Executive leadership mandates a transition to a platform-based business model, encouraging third-party developers to build extensions on top of your core software.

options.text: Build restrictive APIs that limit third-party developer access to protect internal code IP.
Design a strategic developer ecosystem platform roadmap, building secure public APIs, robust developer documentation, and clear integration governance frameworks.
Refuse to open platform access, arguing that third-party integrations introduce security risks.
Open all internal databases to external developers without access controls or documentation.

scenario: Your organization is experiencing rapid growth through multi-national expansion, but your team's operational systems are heavily centralized and lack regional customization support.

options.text: Force regional offices to adapt their operational workflows to match your centralized system constraints.
Re-architect your department's operational system model toward a flexible, multi-tenant framework that balances global standards with regional autonomy.
Allow each regional office to purchase and build their own independent operational software systems.
Build custom code forks for every new region, increasing long-term technical debt and maintenance complexity.

scenario: You discover a major miscalculation in a quarterly report that your department already submitted to executive leadership. Correcting the error will reduce your team's reported achievements and cause you to miss a key target.

options.text: Promptly notify executive leadership of the error, present the corrected metrics along with a root-cause analysis, and outline actionable steps to prevent similar miscalculations.
Quietly update the metrics in next quarter's report without explicitly pointing out the previous miscalculation to leadership.
Ignore the error since the report was already approved and nobody outside your department has noticed it.
Inform your direct supervisor privately about the error and let them decide whether it needs to be escalated to executive leadership.

scenario: A high-performing direct report routinely turns in exceptional technical work but consistently skips mandatory compliance tracking and time-logging protocols, claiming it hinders their productivity.

options.text: Exempt the employee from compliance logging so they can remain focused on delivering high-value technical work.
Meet with the employee to emphasize that compliance and Integrity standards apply equally to everyone, establish clear expectations, and hold them accountable in performance reviews.
Ask a junior team member to fill out the high performer's compliance logs for them.
Issue an immediate formal written warning without discussing the underlying reasons for non-compliance with the employee.

scenario: During a key product launch, your team misses a critical deadline due to an oversight you made during sprint planning. Your director assumes the delay was caused by a vendor failure.

options.text: Let the director blame the vendor to protect your team's reputation and standing within the company.
Take direct accountability with your director for the planning oversight, present a revised delivery timeline, and share the mitigation plan.
Correct the director privately, but mention that the vendor's slow responses contributed to your oversight.
Blame the frontline team members for not flagging the planning bottleneck earlier.

scenario: You oversee a vendor selection process. One of the top-bidding vendors is owned by a personal friend, though their proposal is genuinely competitive.

options.text: Formally disclose the conflict of interest to procurement and leadership immediately, and recuse yourself from the final evaluation and decision-making panel.
Proceed with evaluating the vendor normally without disclosing the friendship, since their proposal is legitimately competitive.
Disqualify your friend's firm quietly to avoid any perception of favoritism, even if they have a great bid.
Inform your panel members of the friendship verbally, but continue serving as the primary decision-maker on the bid.

scenario: Your manager asks you to manipulate project status dashboard indicators from 'Red' to 'Green' to make the department look better during an upcoming board audit.

options.text: Comply with your manager's request, as refusing a direct order from your supervisor is insubordination.
Respectfully decline to alter the status, explain the risk of misleading the board, and offer to help prepare a transparent recovery plan to present alongside the 'Red' status.
Change the status to 'Yellow' as a compromise to satisfy your manager while acknowledging some risk.
Bypass your manager and immediately report them to the ethics hotline without attempting a direct conversation first.

scenario: A cross-functional project fails to deliver its core outcomes. The other department head publicly blames your team, but internal records show both teams contributed equally to the failure.

options.text: Publicly attack the other department head in an email blast to expose their team's specific failures.
Acknowledge your team's specific share of the shortcomings, present objective project logs to clarify the shared responsibility, and focus the discussion on joint remediation.
Accept total blame for the entire failure to maintain peace and end the public argument quickly.
Schedule a private meeting with the other department head to align on a shared, blameless narrative before responding to stakeholders.

scenario: You notice that an employee reporting to you has been claiming expense reimbursements for client dinners that exceed policy limits by splitting receipts into smaller transactions.

options.text: Ignore the policy breach because the dinners were genuinely with real clients and brought in business.
Address the policy violation immediately in a private meeting, require reimbursement of unauthorized claims, and report the non-compliance according to corporate policy.
Approve the current expenses but warn the employee verbally never to split receipts again.
Reject the expense claims without talking to the employee and let HR handle any follow-up.

scenario: Your team accidentally receives confidential salary and rating data for another department due to an email misdirection by HR.

options.text: Delete the file immediately, notify HR of the misdirection, and instruct your team members who saw it to keep the information strictly confidential.
Review the file to compare your team's compensation against the other department before deleting it.
Forward the email back to HR explaining the mistake, but keep a saved copy just in case compensation disputes arise later.
Notify HR of the error and ask them how you should handle the situation before taking any action.

scenario: An initiative championed by your team is falling well short of its projected ROI. Admitting this now will likely result in the project's cancellation and budget reduction for your unit.

options.text: Present the actual performance data transparently to leadership, recommend winding down or pivoting the initiative, and reallocate remaining resources to higher-impact work.
Adjust performance projection formulas to make the initiative appear on track for another two quarters.
Slow down project spending quietly and hope leadership forgets about the initial ROI targets.
Ask leadership for a budget increase, arguing that additional funding is required to reach the original ROI targets.

scenario: You observe a peer manager taking credit for a complex strategic framework that was actually created by a junior staff member on your team.

options.text: Publicly call out the peer manager during an executive presentation to embarrass them for stealing work.
Speak with the peer manager privately to advocate for proper attribution, and ensure the junior staff member is highlighted in upcoming project communications and reviews.
Say nothing, as questioning a peer manager's Integrity damages cross-departmental relationships.
Advise the junior employee to lodge a formal complaint with HR regarding the stolen work.

scenario: Your team discovers a security vulnerability in a software product that is scheduled for commercial release tomorrow. Fixing it will delay the release by two weeks.

options.text: Proceed with the release on schedule and release a silent security patch in a future update.
Halt the release, inform stakeholders transparently about the vulnerability, and prioritize the resolution to safeguard user trust and product security.
Ask your engineers if there is a quick band-aid fix that can be applied in two hours, regardless of long-term stability.
Escalate the finding to executive leadership and let them decide whether to ship with the known vulnerability.

scenario: A direct report brings you evidence that a key client is regularly violating safety or ethical protocols set out in your contract, but this client accounts for 30% of your revenue.

options.text: Ignore the report because losing 30% of your revenue would lead to budget cuts and potential layoffs in your team.
Document the violations, schedule an executive meeting with the client to insist on strict adherence to protocols, and prepare an exit plan if compliance is refused.
Tell your direct report to handle it informally with the client's operational team without escalating.
Report the client directly to legal/compliance and let them handle all future communications.

scenario: You made a promise to your team that if they met a difficult quarterly milestone, you would secure a specific bonus or perk. The team hit the milestone, but executive leadership denied the perk.

options.text: Tell the team that leadership doesn't care about their hard work and blame upper management entirely.
Take accountability for making a promise before securing formal executive approval, apologize to the team, and work to find alternative, approved ways to recognize their achievement.
Pretend you never guaranteed the perk and tell the team they misunderstood your original statement.
Use your own discretionary budget quietly to fund the perk without telling leadership.

scenario: You discover that a legacy process in your department accidentally double-counts certain operational efficiency savings, artificially inflating your team's contribution metrics.

options.text: Correct the calculation model immediately, document the impact, and present the updated realistic metrics to leadership.
Leave the process as is until an external auditor catches it.
Gradually adjust the formula over the next three years so the metric drop looks like a natural decline.
Fix the formula for future data entries, but leave all historical reported numbers uncorrected.

scenario: One of your direct reports makes a public mistake in an inter-departmental meeting that reflects poorly on your unit's capability.

options.text: Reprimand the report in front of everyone during the meeting to show you have high standards.
Support the report in the meeting, take team-level responsibility for the output, and coach the individual privately afterward on correcting the mistake.
Say nothing in the meeting, but reassign the project away from the employee immediately afterward.
Correct the report's statement during the meeting neutrally, then hold a private 1-on-1 debrief.

scenario: You are under intense pressure to hit a hiring quota by end of quarter. A candidate's background check reveals a minor compliance discrepancy that HR says you can choose to overlook.

options.text: Overlook the discrepancy and hire the candidate immediately to hit your quarterly quota.
Investigate the discrepancy thoroughly with HR, ask the candidate for clarification, and make a principled decision based on integrity standards rather than quota targets.
Reject the candidate immediately without investigating to ensure zero personal risk.
Pass the decision to your director so you are not personally responsible if something goes wrong.

scenario: A close colleague and peer manager confides in you that they are actively interviewing with a direct competitor and have downloaded internal strategy documents to prepare.

options.text: Keep quiet to protect your friendship, as it is none of your business.
Urge the peer to return or delete the internal documents immediately; if they refuse, report the data security risk to information security/HR.
Tell your mutual boss about their job search, but omit the part about downloading documents.
Confront the peer firmly and demand they inform HR about their exit plan by the end of the week.

scenario: Your team is responsible for managing a budget, and you realize at the end of the fiscal year that you have $50,000 remaining. Company culture encourages 'spending it or losing it' on non-essential items.

options.text: Spend the money on unnecessary high-end equipment to ensure your budget isn't reduced next year.
Return the unspent funds transparently, and build a clear, value-based business case for next year's budget requirements based on actual strategic needs.
Pre-pay future vendor contracts for essential services to utilize the remaining budget legitimately.
Ask your team for ideas on how to spend the funds quickly before the deadline passes.

scenario: You realize that a decision you advocated for six months ago has led to increased operational complexity and higher costs, despite initial projections.

options.text: Acknowledge the negative outcome publicly, analyze the breakdown in initial assumptions, and present a course-correction plan.
Blame the operational teams for executing your decision poorly.
Defend the decision continuously, arguing that more time is needed to see the benefits.
Quietly initiate changes to reverse the decision without making an official announcement.

scenario: During a high-stakes client presentation, a team lead on your staff makes a promise regarding product performance that you know is technically inaccurate.

options.text: Correct the statement gently during the meeting to manage client expectations accurately, and debrief with the team lead afterward.
Interrupt the team lead harshly and tell the client that the team lead doesn't know what they are talking about.
Say nothing during the presentation, and let the client discover the limitation during onboarding.
Allow the presentation to finish, then send a written clarification to the client immediately afterward.

scenario: An influential executive asks you to bypass standard procurement vetting to fast-track a software contract for a vendor they personally recommended.

options.text: Bypass the procurement process completely to keep the executive happy.
Explain the compliance and security risks of bypassing procurement, and offer to work with procurement to expedite the standard review process legally.
Ask procurement to do a fake, superficial check so you can check the box quickly.
Submit the contract through standard channels without telling the executive you declined to bypass the process.

scenario: You oversee a team member who is struggling personally and missing deliverables. Your director instructs you to 'find a reason to fire them' immediately to free up headcount.

options.text: Fabricate performance documentation to justify immediate termination as ordered by your director.
Insist on following fair, documented performance management procedures, offer proper support and clear goals, and communicate this approach transparently to your director.
Reassign the employee's work to others and hope they resign on their own.
Place the employee on an immediate formal PIP while explaining to them privately that the mandate came from above.

scenario: You find out that a feature rolled out by your team collects user location data by default without explicit user consent, violating new privacy standards.

options.text: Disable the default data collection feature immediately, inform leadership and legal, and issue an update requiring explicit user opt-in.
Keep collecting the data until a user formally complains or flags the issue.
Update the privacy policy fine print on the website without changing the software behavior.
Schedule a feature review for the next development cycle in two months to fix the consent flow.

scenario: You are asked to evaluate your department's readiness for a major technology transformation. You know your team is not ready, but admitting it will delay a corporate initiative.

options.text: Report that your team is fully ready to avoid slowing down the corporate initiative.
Provide an honest evaluation of readiness gaps, present a clear timeline for remediation, and advocate for necessary training before rollout.
Give a vague, neutral response that neither confirms nor denies readiness.
State that your team is ready, but add disclaimers that protect you if the transformation fails.

scenario: A vendor offers you free tickets to an exclusive industry conference and paid luxury accommodation, which falls into a grey area of your corporate gift policy.

options.text: Accept the gift and accommodation without reporting it, as it is an industry event.
Consult compliance policy, formally disclose the offer to HR/Legal, and decline or pay for expenses using corporate travel budget if attendance is valuable.
Accept the conference tickets but pay for the hotel yourself to balance things out.
Decline the offer entirely without evaluating if attending the conference has business value for your company.

scenario: Your team's workload has dropped significantly due to automation, but you are concerned that reporting this will reduce your headcount and managerial scope.

options.text: Create artificial tasks and busywork to make your team appear fully occupied.
Report the capacity gains transparently to leadership, and propose redeploying your team's bandwidth to new strategic initiatives.
Keep quiet about the extra bandwidth and let your team work lighter hours quietly.
Offer your team's excess bandwidth to peer managers informally without notifying executive leadership.

scenario: During a performance calibration meeting, other managers are artificially inflating their reports' ratings to secure larger bonus pools. Your team's ratings are accurate.

options.text: Inflate your team's ratings as well so your reports aren't financially disadvantaged.
Maintain your objective ratings, present data-backed evidence for your scores, and advocate for calibration standards to be strictly enforced across all managers.
Lower your team's ratings further to highlight the dishonesty of the other managers.
Escalate the calibration discrepancy to HR after the meeting without speaking up during the calibration discussion.

scenario: You discover that a senior leader in your division has been approving contracts for a consulting firm where their family member is a principal partner.

options.text: Confront the senior leader directly and threaten to report them unless they end the contract.
Report the potential conflict of interest through formal internal compliance or whistleblower channels with supporting documentation.
Ignore the situation to avoid jeopardizing your career prospects in the company.
Mention it informally to your manager to see if they are already aware of the relationship.

scenario: Your team delivered a project late. In the post-mortem, two team members start blaming each other for missed handoffs and communication gaps.

options.text: Take ultimate accountability as manager for process breakdowns, guide the post-mortem toward objective root causes, and establish clear handoff SLAs moving forward.
Pick one employee to take the blame publicly so the team can move on.
End the meeting and issue written warnings to both employees for failing to collaborate.
Let them argue it out in the meeting until they agree on who was at fault.

scenario: You realize that a policy you strictly enforced last month was based on your misunderstanding of a new HR mandate, causing unnecessary stress for your team.

options.text: Pretend the HR policy changed again this month so you don't have to admit you made a mistake.
Address the team openly, acknowledge your misunderstanding, apologize for the unnecessary burden, and clarify the correct policy.
Quietly stop enforcing the policy and hope nobody asks questions about it.
Blame HR for sending confusing documentation that led to your misinterpretation.

scenario: A key client offers to write a glowing public testimonial for your team, but asks you to inflate certain metric results in the case study draft.

options.text: Accept the inflated metrics in the draft because a public testimonial is great for marketing.
Politely decline to inflate the numbers, explain your commitment to accurate reporting, and offer a case study focused on genuine, verified metrics.
Publish the case study without any metrics at all to avoid the disagreement.
Cancel the testimonial project entirely without explaining why to the client.

scenario: An offshore development partner delivers code that passes automated testing but contains severe architectural shortcuts that violate your internal quality standards.

options.text: Accept the code as is to hit project milestone dates and plan to refactor it later.
Reject the deliverable, conduct a review with the partner lead to detail the architectural violations, and enforce quality standards before sign-off.
Have your internal team rewrite the code silently to avoid confronting the vendor.
Approve the deliverable but withhold a portion of the payment until they promise to do better next time.

scenario: You are leading a project that involves restructuring your team. You know three roles will be eliminated in two months, but executive leadership has asked for strict confidentiality for now.

options.text: Leak the news informally to the three affected employees so they can start job hunting early.
Honor confidentiality protocols, while actively preparing support structures, severance packages, and transition plans to execute compassionately as soon as announcement approval is granted.
Lie directly to team members if they ask about rumors, promising them that no jobs will be lost.
Push leadership to authorize immediate disclosure, and defer all team planning until approval is given.

scenario: Your department is experiencing unprecedented workload pressure due to back-to-back project launches, and you notice clear signs of physical fatigue and irritability in yourself during daily meetings.

options.text: Acknowledge your stress, establish firm personal boundary habits (such as stepping away for short breaks), and model healthy workload management while delegating key operational tasks.
Push through the fatigue by working late hours to show the team that managers must lead by sacrifice.
Hide your exhaustion behind a forced cheerful demeanor while continuing to handle all current tasks without adjustment.
Take an unexpected week-off immediately without setting up interim coverage for your direct reports.

scenario: A high-stakes initiative that your team spent four months preparing is abruptly cancelled by senior leadership due to unexpected budget cuts, leaving your team feeling demoralized and defeated.

options.text: Validate the team's disappointment, facilitate a constructive debrief to extract key learnings, and pivot their focus to how those learnings directly advance upcoming strategic priorities.
Tell the team that cancellations are a normal part of business and insist they immediately start the next project without dwelling on the past.
Join in with the team's complaints about senior management to demonstrate empathy and build solidarity.
Give the entire team two days off without informing senior management or arranging coverage.

scenario: During a high-stakes executive review, a senior stakeholder harshly criticizes your department's strategy using aggressive, emotional language in front of your peers.

options.text: Maintain emotional composure, listen calmly without reacting defensively, acknowledge the core underlying concerns, and request a follow-up session to review data objectively.
Respond with equal aggression to defend your team's honor and ensure you are not seen as weak.
Accept all criticisms silently without standing up for your strategy, and agree to change the plan immediately.
Politely ask to pause the presentation and suggest resuming the discussion privately after a short break.

scenario: You are managing three critical, competing deadlines due in the same week, and several key staff members are simultaneously out on unplanned sick leave.

options.text: Audit project commitments, communicate capacity limits transparently to stakeholders, negotiate scope reductions or staggered delivery dates, and focus team energy on core priorities.
Require the remaining team members to work mandatory overtime and weekends to hit all original deadlines.
Do all the extra operational work yourself late into the night to protect your team from extra stress.
Inform stakeholders that deadlines will be missed across all three projects without offering a revised delivery plan.

scenario: A key team lead who handles a sole-dependency function is showing severe burnout symptoms and threatens to resign if their workload is not reduced immediately.

options.text: Hold an empathetic check-in, temporarily reallocate non-essential tasks to unblock them, and build a cross-training plan to eliminate single-person dependencies.
Offer them a financial bonus to incentivize them to stay and finish the current crunch period.
Tell them everyone is under stress and that quitting during a critical sprint shows a lack of commitment.
Approve an immediate leave of absence without reallocating their tasks, causing project deliverables to stall.

scenario: Your organization is undergoing a prolonged corporate merger with frequent rumors of restructuring, causing chronic anxiety and productivity drops across your team.

options.text: Establish a predictable communication cadence, focus the team on controllable day-to-day outcomes, and provide a safe space for them to voice concerns.
Reassure the team that no one will be laid off, even though you do not have executive confirmation of job security.
Avoid discussing the merger entirely during team meetings to prevent escalating anxiety.
Tell the team that worrying is unproductive and enforce stricter daily output tracking.

scenario: You receive critical, unexpected negative feedback regarding your leadership style from your direct reports during an annual 360-degree performance review.

options.text: Process the emotional reaction privately, thank the team for their honesty, discuss key feedback areas openly, and co-create an improvement plan with measurable check-ins.
Defend your management style in the next team meeting, explaining why your decisions were necessary for team success.
Try to figure out which specific employees gave negative ratings and treat them with caution.
Acknowledge the feedback briefly in an email and promise to make adjustments without further group discussion.

scenario: A major production system outage occurs during a peak business period, causing panic among stakeholders and high tension among your technical resolution team.

options.text: Maintain a calm demeanor, establish clear triage roles, shield the technical team from non-essential stakeholder interruptions, and provide periodic factual updates.
Micromanage the engineers' minute-by-minute progress to ensure the system comes back online as fast as possible.
Express panic openly so the team understands the extreme urgency and severity of the outage.
Take over fixing the technical problem yourself while ignoring stakeholder communication completely.

scenario: Your department is subjected to constant, rapid strategy shifts from upper management, making long-term planning feel impossible and exhausting your staff.

options.text: Filter out non-essential operational noise, build flexible sprint cycles focused on adaptable core capabilities, and help the team find stability in short-term milestones.
Pass every single executive communication and strategy change directly to the team as soon as you receive it.
Refuse to implement new strategy shifts until upper management guarantees a freeze on further changes.
Complain with the team about leadership's inconsistency while executing the bare minimum required.

scenario: You are balancing a high-stress personal life event alongside a major quarterly deliverable at work, and you feel your focus slipping.

options.text: Communicate proactively with your direct supervisor about your situation, delegate operational tasks to capable team leads, and leverage flexible work policies.
Try to keep your personal struggles completely secret while attempting to work extra hours to maintain standard output.
Let work tasks slip without notifying anyone, assuming colleagues will naturally step in to cover.
Take emergency leave immediately without delegating core responsibilities or setting up an out-of-office protocol.

scenario: An ongoing interpersonal conflict between two key employees is creating a tense, hostile atmosphere that is draining the energy of the surrounding team.

options.text: Intervene promptly to address the emotional tension, facilitate a structured resolution dialogue, and set clear standards for professional working conduct.
Hope the conflict resolves itself over time as long as both employees continue submitting their individual work.
Reassign one of the employees to a lower-visibility project to eliminate the immediate friction.
Warn both employees that further public disagreement will result in formal HR documentation.

scenario: Your team has successfully delivered a grueling 6-month project that required significant overtime, but executive leadership immediately assigns another urgent project with no downtime.

options.text: Advocate firmly with leadership for a recovery period, negotiate adjusted timelines for the new project, and build in time to celebrate the team's recent achievement.
Accept the new project timeline immediately and demand the team maintain their crunch-mode momentum.
Tell the team that leadership doesn't care about their fatigue, but encourage them to push through anyway.
Allow the team to work at a very slow pace secretly without adjusting official project milestone dates.

scenario: A pilot project you personally advocated for fails to achieve its primary metrics, resulting in lost budget and public scrutiny from peer managers.

options.text: Take accountability for the failure, extract key operational insights, share a transparent post-mortem with stakeholders, and pivot to a revised strategy.
Blame the failure on poor execution by frontline staff or unexpected external vendor delays.
Downplay the negative metrics and highlight minor positive vanity metrics to defend the project's success.
Acknowledge the failure briefly and immediately change the subject to future initiatives.

scenario: You notice an increase in minor careless errors and absenteeism across your department following a period of sustained high pressure.

options.text: Recognize the systemic stress, conduct a workload assessment, review deadlines with stakeholders, and actively promote wellbeing and time-off resources.
Issue formal written warnings to employees making errors to enforce quality standards.
Ignore the trend, assuming error rates will return to baseline once the stress naturally subsides.
Implement daily quality audits to catch and correct employee errors before work is finalized.

scenario: You are pitch-preparing for an executive budget defense meeting. An hour before the meeting, your primary data model gets corrupted.

options.text: Stay calm, utilize backup summaries or high-level estimates, inform the executive panel transparently of the technical glitch, and offer to follow up with detailed figures.
Cancel the budget meeting immediately, risking losing your budget allocation slot for the upcoming fiscal year.
Panic and try to guess numbers during the presentation, hoping the board won't notice inaccuracies.
Ask a team lead to present in your place using whatever partial notes remain available.

scenario: Your team's physical environment or digital workspace undergoes a sudden, poorly executed platform change that severely slows down daily task execution.

options.text: Acknowledge the operational frustration, establish manual workarounds for critical paths, and advocate with IT for system enhancements while maintaining morale.
Tell the team to stop complaining and adapt to the new tool regardless of its performance limitations.
Authorize your team to bypass IT security and use unauthorized personal tools to keep speed up.
Allow output metrics to drop significantly without setting up workarounds or notifying leadership.

scenario: A high-value client threatens to terminate their contract due to a service error made by your team, creating intense stress for your account managers.

options.text: Support the account managers directly, join the client conversation as an executive sponsor, take accountability, and outline a robust remediation framework.
Leave the account managers to handle the client alone so they learn how to manage high-stress situations.
Publicly discipline the employee who made the original service error to appease the client.
Offer the client an immediate, steep financial discount without investigating the root cause of the error.

scenario: You feel overwhelmed by an influx of daily administrative demands, meeting invites, and slack notifications, leaving no time for strategic management tasks.

options.text: Audit your time usage, decline non-essential meetings, establish daily focused focus-time blocks, and streamline administrative reporting channels.
Work longer hours into the night to clear your inbox and complete administrative tasks.
Stop responding to messages and emails from peer departments to protect your personal time.
Delegate all your administrative duties to direct reports, even if it overload their schedules.

scenario: Your department is tasked with executing a high-visibility project using a technology stack that your team has zero experience with, and the deadline is tight.

options.text: Frame the project as a strategic learning opportunity, secure rapid training or expert advisory support, and negotiate phased delivery risks with leadership.
Refuse the project outright, stating that your team lacks the necessary qualifications.
Expect the team to learn the new technology in their personal time while maintaining standard sprint speed.
Outsource the technical build completely without upskilling internal staff.

scenario: A key stakeholder repeatedly expresses cynicism about your team's capability during cross-functional meetings, creating ongoing frustration for your reports.

options.text: Schedule a private 1-on-1 with the stakeholder to understand their underlying concerns, establish objective communication channels, and reassure your team offline.
Confront the stakeholder aggressively during a public meeting to demand they respect your team.
Instruct your team to ignore the stakeholder's feedback entirely.
Escalate the stakeholder's behavior to executive management without trying to resolve it directly first.

scenario: You notice that your personal motivation and energy levels have dropped significantly over the past quarter, making routine decision-making feel daunting.

options.text: Recognize early signs of manager burnout, consult professional support or mentor guidance, delegate routine operational decisions, and take planned leave.
Ignore the feelings and force yourself to make quick decisions to maintain the appearance of strong leadership.
Abdictate decision-making entirely to direct reports without providing clear guidance or frameworks.
Inform your team that you are feeling unmotivated and ask them to lower output expectations for a while.

scenario: Your team experiences two consecutive quarterly targets misses, and senior leadership demands an immediate explanation and turnaround plan.

options.text: Lead a objective diagnostic review with the team, present a transparent turnaround plan to leadership focusing on systemic root causes, and maintain team confidence.
Blame market conditions and corporate budget restrictions entirely for the missed targets.
Blame underperforming individual team members during the leadership update to shield yourself.
Commit to unrealistic, doubled targets for next quarter to prove your department's resilience.

scenario: A sudden organizational restructuring assigns two struggling, low-performing sub-units under your direct management scope.

options.text: Approach the addition with a constructive mindset, evaluate talent and process bottlenecks objectively, establish clear performance benchmarks, and offer structured coaching.
Complain to HR that taking on underperforming units is unfair to your current performance track record.
Immediately place low-performing staff in those units on performance improvement plans without prior evaluation.
Keep the new units completely separate from your high-performing team to prevent negative cultural contagion.

scenario: During a period of high organizational stress, rumors spread that your department's function is going to be outsourced to an external agency.

options.text: Address the rumors transparently, share verified information from executive leadership, clarify what is known and unknown, and anchor the team on core deliverables.
Deny the rumors categorically, even if you do not have official confirmation from executive leadership.
Refuse to comment on the rumors, stating that corporate discussions are confidential.
Encourage staff to start updating their resumes privately just in case the rumors are true.

scenario: You are delivering a complex, long-term project, and key requirements change significantly every month, disrupting current sprint cycles.

options.text: Implement an agile change-control mechanism, establish clear trade-off protocols with stakeholders for new requests, and coach the team on adaptable building practices.
Refuse all change requests after the initial project scope is signed off to protect team stability.
Accept every change request without adjusting delivery dates, pushing the team to adapt faster.
Pause the project completely until stakeholders promise to stop changing requirements.

scenario: An key vendor fails to deliver critical components on time, threatening an upcoming client product release.

options.text: Activate contingency plans, explore secondary supplier options or technical workarounds, and communicate revised risk profiles proactively to stakeholders.
Wait for the primary vendor to fix their delivery issues while hoping the delay is minimal.
Cancel the product release entirely and blame the vendor in public communications.
Demand that your internal team build the vendor's components from scratch overnight.

scenario: Your department is operating under a strict budget freeze, preventing you from hiring replacement staff for two employees who recently left.

options.text: Re-evaluate department capacity, prioritize core revenue or compliance drivers, trim low-impact activities, and renegotiate deliverable dates with leadership.
Force remaining team members to absorb all duties of the departing staff without modifying project scope.
Stop delivering on lower-priority projects without communicating changes to internal stakeholders.
Hire unapproved contractors and attempt to cover costs through petty expense channels.

scenario: You receive public criticism from a peer manager during a multi-departmental leadership meeting regarding your team's operational speed.

options.text: Maintain professional poise, offer a succinct factual response regarding quality and compliance standards, and suggest a private sync to review operational metrics.
Immediately criticize the peer manager's department quality errors to balance the conversation.
Apologize profusely in front of everyone and promise that your team will work faster immediately.
Remain silent during the meeting, but write a complaining email to your shared director afterward.

scenario: Your team has experienced a string of small operational failures over the past month, causing confidence and enthusiasm to drop sharply.

options.text: Host a blameless retrospective to identify systemic failure patterns, highlight recent small wins to rebuild momentum, and establish achievable, short-term targets.
Reprimand the team for lacking attention to detail and demand higher focus.
Ignore the small failures and act as if everything is going perfectly to keep energy up.
Take over executing critical project steps yourself to prevent further operational failures.

scenario: You are managing a remote team, and you notice that team members are answering Slack messages late at night and working through weekends continuously.

options.text: Establish clear department guidelines regarding communication boundaries, discourage after-hours messaging, and model sustainable work habits yourself.
Praise the employees publicly in team channels for their dedication and round-the-clock availability.
Ignore the behavior as long as project deadlines are being met ahead of schedule.
Turn off department communication channels entirely after 6 PM to force compliance.

scenario: Executive management introduces a mandatory time-tracking tool that requires staff to log activities in 15-minute increments, creating widespread anger and stress.

options.text: Acknowledge the team's frustration, explain the organizational context (e.g., client billing/resource planning), streamline tracking workflows, and focus on outcomes.
Tell the team that corporate rules must be followed without complaint and threaten disciplinary action for non-compliance.
Secretly tell the team to fill in fake data just to satisfy the corporate requirement.
Fill out the 15-minute time logs for your entire team yourself to shield them from the stress.

scenario: You are pitched with a major crisis, a high-stakes executive request, and a severe client escalation all happening within the same hour.

options.text: Take a moment to regulate your response, rapidly assess risk and urgency across all three events, delegate clear sub-tasks to key leads, and communicate triage steps.
Attempt to solve all three problems simultaneously by multi-tasking rapidly.
Focus entirely on the executive request to protect your standing, leaving the crisis and client escalation unattended.
Escalate all three issues directly to your director, stating that the situation is unmanageable.

scenario: After months of intense effort, a key client decides to non-renew their contract for reasons completely outside your team's control (e.g., client corporate liquidation).

options.text: Reinforce to the team that their execution was high quality, frame the loss constructively, and redirect the team's energy toward pipeline growth and current accounts.
Conduct a harsh review meeting to criticize team members for not saving the account.
Avoid bringing up the account loss to prevent lowering department morale.
Send a brief email announcing the loss and move on immediately without addressing the emotional impact on the team.
